messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays half a step behind Bram, hands loose and empty where the guards can see them, and lets the big man's mail do the talking for a moment. Then he pulls Hesta Corl's letter from inside his jerkin and holds it up, unfolded, without handing it over.

"We do, friend. Mistress Corl's business. Her late brother's deed box, from his office. Hers by right, and the letter says so, sealed and signed." He nods at the bright new lock. "Your masters can keep the wool, the barrels, the rats, all of it. We want one iron box, and you can watch us carry it out so nobody says we took a spoon."

While he talks, his eyes don't stay on the broad one. He's watching the thin guard: where he keeps looking down the street, what he's waiting for, whether he's nervous about *us* or about someone else. Without making a show of it, he also takes in that shutter hanging open up top, the wall beneath it, and what handholds there are.

If the broad one reaches for the letter, Pell lets him read it but keeps a finger on the corner.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stop a few paces short of the men, keeping my sword sheathed.

“Aye. Hesta Corl sent us for her iron deed box from her brother’s office. We’ve a letter of claim.” I nod toward Pell. “Not here to shift wool or empty the place. Who’s authorised to let us collect it?”

While we talk, I keep an eye on the thin guard and the stretch of street he’s watching.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text: Sefa steps forward a half-pace, empty hands held low, the gesture open and tired rather than bold. "We've a letter of claim from Hesta Corl," she says. "Her brother's deed box is hers by right — you know it is, or you'd not be standing outside like men waiting for dawn instead of dragging it back to whoever pays you. We're not here for trouble. We're here to take what's already hers and go."

scenes.narration:
A lantern hangs on a hook by the warehouse door, and the broad guard steps into its light so they can see he means it. Down the Coast Way a few forges are still going late, red mouths in the dark, hammers ringing out of time with each other.

He looks at the letter Pell holds up and doesn't reach for it. His lips move over the first line, slowly, then he gives up and looks at the seal instead. "That's her seal, right enough," he says. "Corl. I seen it on wool bales." He turns to Bram and takes in the shield, the stance, the way Bram stopped short with his hand off the hilt. Something in his face settles. "You've walked behind wagons."

Then he answers what was asked, without hurrying. "Who's authorised. Mr Oake. Dalmar Oake, the moneylender. He bought the dead man's paper, all of it, and he pays me to stand here. Nobody goes in. That's the order, and it's the whole of the order." He nods at Sefa. "You may be right that it's hers, mistress. I don't say you're not. I'm not the court. The court sits at dawn, and you can wave that letter at the magistrate there and see what he makes of it." He scratches his jaw. "And Oake's clerk came by at lamp-lighting and said it particular: nobody in the office. Not the lads, not me. So that box matters to somebody besides your mistress."

The thin one hasn't said a word yet. Pell, watching him, sees a man who hardly looks at the three of them. His eyes keep going south down the Way, toward where the street bends past a cooper's yard. When a boy's footsteps slap across the cobbles somewhere out of sight he stiffens, half turns, and sags again when nobody comes round the corner. He's wound tight, but not about them. He looks like a man waiting for somebody to arrive, and running out of patience.

"Gorm's told you," he says at last, short and flat, still looking down the street. "Oake keeps his counting-room on Smithy Row, over the chandler's. Go and bother him. He's likely abed." He shifts his weight. "And there's four more of us across the yard if you want to make a night of it."

He tips his head at the loading yard beside the warehouse. Across it, behind a low wall, stands a narrow two-storey lodging with one window lit and a shadow moving behind the shutter.

Pell has the wall read in the time it takes the thin man to talk. The open shutter is about fifteen feet up, on the street face just short of the corner where the yard begins. Below it the stone runs to about head height, and above that timber framing is set between the courses, its beam-ends jutting a few inches out of the wall. A rain gutter's iron downpipe runs from the eaves to the yard corner. To him it's a staircase, if nobody is standing under it with a lantern. Right now Gorm Hadley is standing under it with a lantern.

Gorm folds his arms, not unkindly, and leans back against the doorpost beside the bright new lock.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Ten years behind wagons,” I tell Gorm. “Long enough to appreciate a plain order.”

I glance toward the southern bend, then back to the thin guard. “But you’ve scarcely looked at us. Who are you expecting from that way? If someone’s coming for the office, we’d best settle whose business takes precedence before they arrive.”

I keep my tone matter-of-fact and my hands clear of my weapons, watching how he takes the question.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds Gorm’s eye a moment, then gives a small, tired nod, as if the answer settles it. “Then we’ll not make a night of it,” she says. She turns and walks a few unhurried steps off along the street, beckoning Bram and Pell with a tilt of her head as though they’ve decided to leave.

When the three of you are far enough that the guards can’t hear, she stops in the shadow of the cooper’s yard wall and speaks low. “There’s a shutter high up that’s open a finger’s width. Pell, if you can get to it, that may be our way in—quiet, while the big one watches the door and the other one watches the road for whoever he’s afraid is coming.” She glances back toward the warehouse. “I can give them something to look at. A sound, a light. And I can keep the box-carriers honest once we’re inside.” She looks between the two of them. “That, or we knock on Oake’s counting-room door at this hour and hope he’s a soft touch. I’d rather not.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell folds the letter and tucks it back inside his jerkin without arguing.

"Fair enough, Gorm. You're paid to stand, and you stand. Smithy Row, over the chandler's." He touches two fingers to his brow. "Sorry to keep you from your night."

As he turns away he passes close to the thin one. With his hand low at his hip, out of the lantern's light, he flicks the old Lower City sign: thumb across two knuckles, then a tap on the wrist. In the cant it means *who are you waiting on?* Anyone guild-raised would know it. Pell doesn't stop or look back. He only watches from the corner of his eye to see whether the man catches it, freezes, or looks blank.

Then he walks with Bram and Sefa back up the Coast Way, out of the lantern's reach and past the first forge's glow, and stops where the hammering covers voices.

"Two things," he says quietly. "Oake told them nobody goes in the office. Not the warehouse, the *office*. And skinny there isn't guarding the door. He's waiting for somebody to come down from the south, past the cooper's. I'd bet a silver they mean to beat us to that box tonight, or he's let them in before."

He jerks his chin back toward the warehouse. "There's an open shutter fifteen feet up, near the yard corner. Beam-ends and a downpipe to get there. I can be up and in without a sound if nobody's lantern is pointing at it. What I need is Gorm looking the other way for a few minutes, and someone watching that bend in the street so we know who turns up."

He looks between them. "Bram, he likes you. He knows you've walked behind wagons. Could you go back and talk road with him, ask about Oake or who else has been by? Sefa, could you watch the cooper's corner and whistle if anyone comes? I'll slip round the far side and come at the wall from the yard end. If the box is up there, I hand it down. If it's not, we know someone's been ahead of us."

"Unless either of you would rather wake the moneylender first. I'd rather not leave it till his clerk's had the night."

Gorm takes Bram's ten years with a slow nod. "Ten. I done four, out of Nashkel. Iron, mostly, and it don't run off in the night." That seems to be all the welcome he gives, and it's plainly meant as one.

Behind him the warehouse door stands in its lantern light, with two men beside it. Past the bend the road south is still empty.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa eases back against the shadowed wall and lets the hammer-fall from the open forge cover the moment while she studies the way things stand. She watches Bram still by the lantern, the line of Gorm’s shoulders, and the lit window beyond the low wall with its patient, passing shadow.

She keeps her voice to Pell, almost under the noise of the forge. “One awake across the yard. If they call out, we’re finished before we start.” A glance toward the roof of the warehouse. “That shutter’s no use to me, but I can follow where you go. And if we’re seen, I’d rather they saw something holy than a coin purse.” She touches the prayer beads at her wrist, not as a gesture, but simply to settle them against the studs of her armour. “What’s your notion for reaching it quiet?”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell crouches beside Sefa in the stave-shadow and keeps his voice under the hammering.

"Bram's still at the door, and that'll do fine. Gorm's happy talking wagons. Stay here. You can see the bend and that lit window both. Anyone comes round the corner, or that lodging door opens, give one short whistle. Two if it's trouble. If I hear two, I go quiet and stay put till it passes." He tugs his hood up. "If it all goes wrong, I come down the yard side and meet you here."

Then he's gone, keeping low. He doesn't cross back through Gorm's lantern-fan. He swings wide along the dark side of the street and comes at the yard from the south end, where the light dies. He keeps to the walls and stays off the cobbles' crown.

At the plank gates he stops and puts his eye to a crack before anything else. Is there anyone in the yard, a dog, a cart, anything that would make noise? He also wants to know how much of the yard corner that lodging window actually sees.

If it's clear, he slips over the low wall where it meets the warehouse, out of the window's line if he can manage it, and goes up the downpipe, testing each bracket before he trusts it, then switching to the beam-ends to reach the shutter. He doesn't touch the shutter at first. He hangs beside the gap and listens, and looks in if there's any light to see by. He's checking for anyone already inside, a lamp, anything moving in that office.

He's in no hurry. He keeps the hooded lantern shut and his hands free.

scenes.narration:
Sefa's words go no farther than Pell under the forge's hammering. He answers her low, pulls his hood up, and leaves the shadow of the staves.

He doesn't go back through the lantern light. He crosses to the far side of the Coast Way, where the house fronts are dark, and drifts north along them in short stops and starts, like a man who belongs on a street at this hour. He comes back across where Gorm's light gives out. The plank gates of the loading yard are shut on their crossbar, and he puts his eye to the gap between two boards.

The yard is beaten earth with straw trodden into it, about forty feet across. There's no dog, no cart and no horse. Against the warehouse's yard wall stand its loading doors, double and barred, and a stack of crates sits beside them under a sheet of oiled canvas weighted at the corners with bricks. Across the yard the lodging's window throws its thin bar of light over the ground at an angle. Pell watches the shadow behind it pass twice, and follows where the line falls. It covers the middle of the yard and the gates. It doesn't reach the corner where the low wall meets the warehouse. The shutter's own frame cuts the man's view short there.

Pell goes over the low wall at that corner. The coping is cold and gritty under his hands and he makes no sound. The downpipe is old iron fixed with brackets at every course. He tests the first with his weight before he trusts it, then the next. One gives a little and he leaves it alone and moves his foot to a beam-end instead. After that he climbs the timber framing, stepping from beam-end to beam-end, quick and sure as he was on the roofs above the Wide. Within a few breaths he is fifteen feet up, flat against the timbers beside the open shutter, with his weight on a beam-end and one hand hooked over a joist.

Down at the forge the apprentices stop. The big piece of iron goes into the trough with a long hiss and a gout of steam. For three or four heartbeats the Coast Way is quiet enough for Sefa to hear the lantern hissing at the warehouse door, the dog somewhere among the yards, and her own breath. Behind the lodging shutter the shadow stops. Then the tongs ring on the anvil, the hammers start again, and the shadow moves on.

Pell hangs beside the gap and listens. Nothing moves inside. There's no lamp and no breathing, only the slow tick of old timber cooling at night. The air through the gap smells of raw wool and lanolin, dust and cold ashes. Through a finger's width of black he can make out nothing beyond the sill. He can feel one thing with a fingertip, though, without pushing: the shutter isn't loose. It's held from inside by a hook in its eye, and the hook is set short, so the shutter stands open a finger's width and no more. Someone set it like that on purpose, and Pell can't tell from here whether it was for air or for something else.

Below him the yard is empty. The bar of light from the lodging lies across the straw where it did before. Sefa stands in the stave-shadow at the cooper's wall with the bend in front of her. The road south beyond it is still empty, and so far no foot has come round it.

scenes.narration:
Bram says it low, close to the stone, and the hammering from the forge carries it no farther than the stave-shadow. Then he settles in against the cooper's wall with his shield turned in to his body, so the iron rim sits clear of the stone and makes no noise.

From here he can see the whole of it. Gorm's lantern still makes its yellow fan on the street face, reaching the bright lock and thinning out toward the corner. Past the corner the downpipe runs down into black. If anything is moving up there against the timbers, the dark keeps it, and Bram can't pick out more than the line of the beam-ends where the red glow from the forge touches them. The plank gates of the loading yard stand shut on their crossbar. Behind them the lodging's thin bar of light lies at its angle, and the shadow behind the shutter crosses it once, slowly, and goes back.

At the door Tobin has hardly moved. He's still facing south, which now means facing the bend and the cooper's wall. His eyes slide over the shadow where Bram stands without stopping on it. He's watching the road beyond.

Then, under the forge's rhythm, Bram hears something he's heard at the end of a thousand days on the Way: iron tyres on cobbles and the slow clop of one heavy horse. It's coming from the north, well up the Coast Way past the warehouse and not yet in sight. Far up the street a single lantern swings low and level, at about the height of a driver's bench, and comes on at a walking pace with no hurry in it.

Gorm hears it too. He pushes off the doorpost and turns his head to look up the street. Tobin doesn't turn at all.

messages.text:
Sefa stays in the wall’s shadow, her shoulders quiet against the stave-stack. She breathes through her nose and lets her attention move in a slow, deliberate pass: the bend south, empty; the forge glow licking at the dark; the lit window across the yard, that restless shadow; Bram by the lantern, keeping the guards in talk; now and then the corner of the warehouse where Pell should show.

She doesn’t move from the watch. Her right hand rests on the cord of her prayer beads, not praying, just ready.

scenes.narration:
Sefa keeps to the dark beside the staves. Her eyes go round and round the same few places, unhurried.

The bend south is empty. The road past it runs pale under the stars to the last houses of town, and nothing moves on it but a cat crossing from one yard wall to the next. The forge glow comes and goes on the cobbles as the apprentices lift and drop the hammer. Across the loading yard the lodging window still holds its thin bar of light. Up at the warehouse corner, where Pell should be, she sees black timber, a blacker downpipe and nothing else. If he's there, the dark is keeping him.

At the door, Gorm's lantern shows two men: Gorm, broad against the doorpost, and Tobin facing south toward her. Tobin's gaze passes over the cooper's wall and doesn't stop. He's looking at the road behind her.

Then she sees a light where there wasn't one: north, up the Coast Way past the warehouse. It's a single lantern, low and level, swinging a little and coming at a walking pace. Under the hammering she can just make out iron tyres grinding on cobbles and the heavy clop of one horse. Over two or three minutes it comes into the edge of the door lantern's light. It's a flat-bed wagon with high sideboards, drawn by a big grey cob with feathered hooves. The driver is a heavy man in a leather hood, bent over the reins. A second figure sits beside him on the bench, smaller and wrapped in a dark cloak with the hood up. From the way the cloak falls, Sefa thinks it may be a woman, but she can't be sure at this distance.

Gorm has stepped off the doorpost and out into the road with his lantern raised. The wagon stops short of him. The cloaked figure leans down from the bench to speak, and Gorm scratches his jaw. Sefa can't hear a word over the forge, only see Gorm's head turning from the cloaked figure to the yard gates and back. Tobin hasn't turned round at all.

Across the yard, the shadow behind the lodging shutter has stopped moving. The thin line of light widens to a hand's breadth as someone inside pushes the shutter open and looks out toward the street.

The bend south is empty. The road past it runs pale under the stars to the last houses of town, and nothing moves on it but a cat crossing from one yard wall to the next. The forge glow comes and goes on the cobbles as the apprentices lift and drop the hammer. Across the loading yard the lodging window still holds its thin bar of light. Up at the warehouse corner, where Pell should be, you see black timber, a blacker downpipe and nothing else. If he's there, the dark is keeping him.

At the door, the lantern shows two men: Gorm, broad against the doorpost, and Tobin facing south toward you. Tobin's gaze passes over the cooper's wall and doesn't stop. He's looking at the road behind you.

Then you see a light where there wasn't one: north, up the Coast Way past the warehouse. It is a single lantern, low and level, swinging a little and coming at a walking pace. Under the hammering you can just make out iron tyres grinding on cobbles and the heavy clop of one horse. Over two or three minutes it comes into the edge of the door lantern's light: a flat-bed wagon with high sideboards, drawn by a big grey cob with feathered hooves. The driver is a heavy man in a leather hood, bent over the reins. A second figure sits beside him on the bench, smaller and wrapped in a dark cloak with the hood up. From the way the cloak falls, you think it may be a woman, but at this distance you can't be sure.

Gorm has stepped off the doorpost and out into the road with his lantern raised. The wagon stops short of him. The cloaked figure leans down from the bench to speak, and Gorm scratches his jaw. You can't hear a word over the forge, only see Gorm's head turning from the cloaked figure to the yard gates and back. Tobin hasn't turned round at all.

Across the yard, the shadow behind the lodging shutter has stopped moving. The thin line of light widens to a hand's breadth as someone inside pushes the shutter open and looks out toward the street.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his weight on the beam-end and works one-handed. From his tools he takes the thin hooked pick, the one for latches rather than locks, and slides it into the gap above the hook's eye. He feels along the hook's shank first. He isn't trying to lift it yet. He's checking whether anything else is tied to it or set on the sill: a thread, a bell, a cup balanced to fall. Someone left this open a finger's width on purpose, and he'd rather know why before he finds out the loud way.

If it's only the hook, he lifts it out of its eye with the pick, slowly, and catches the shutter with his fingers so it can't swing or knock. He waits for the hammers at the forge to be in full swing, opens it just wide enough to fold himself through, and slides in over the sill feet first. Then he crouches below the window and stays still for a count of twenty, listening.

Once he's in, he draws the shutter back to and sets the hook in its eye at the same short reach it had before. From the yard or the street it should look exactly as it did. If someone's coming to use this window tonight, he doesn't want them warned.

Only then does he crack the hooded lantern, a sliver of light, aimed at the floor and shielded by his body from the shutter gap. He wants to see where he is and whether the dust on the floor has fresh footprints in it. If it does, he notes which way they go and how many there are before he takes a step.

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps his weight on the beam-end and slides the thin latch-pick into the gap above the hook's eye. He lays it along the shank as lightly as a fingertip, feeling for anything that shouldn't be there.

The pick finds it at once. A fine wire, wound twice round the shank just under the eye, is drawn taut and runs back along the inside of the frame into the dark. It's thin and smooth, with none of the grit that old iron picks up in a warehouse, so Pell knows it's new. The trouble is that he found it by laying the pick on it, and the wire is set so fine that his touch was enough. It gives by a hair, and he feels it give.

Across the yard a small bell rings in the creditors' lodging: three quick, tinny strokes, clear through the hand's breadth of open shutter. It comes in the half-breath between one hammer-fall and the next, and Pell hears every stroke.

The lodging shutter bangs all the way open. A man leans out with a lamp held at arm's length. His shirt is untied, and he looks at the warehouse wall, not at the street. "The high one!" he shouts back into the room. "That's the high shutter! Up, the lot of you, up!" Boots hit the boards behind him. A second light comes on downstairs, then a third. Somebody swears, a door slams, and somebody else is calling for his boots. The lamp sweeps the yard in a yellow arc across the straw, the canvas over the crates and the barred loading doors. The window frame cuts the light off just short of the corner where Pell hangs. For the moment the frame is still on his side, but men with lanterns won't stay behind a window.

Out on the Coast Way, past the corner, Gorm's voice comes up slow and loud: "What's that? What's the bell?" Then the wagon's iron tyres grind, and the big cob stamps and snorts.

Pell is flat against the timbers fifteen feet up, one hand on a joist and one foot on a beam-end. The pick is still in the gap and the hook is still in its eye. Below him the yard is empty for a few heartbeats more. The lodging door bangs open onto it.

messages.text:
“Wagon coming from the north,” I murmur. “Let’s see where it stops.”

I stay against the wall and watch it approach, looking for any merchant’s mark and whether the driver turns toward the loading yard. I keep the yard gates in view as well—particularly anyone coming out to meet it.

scenes.narration:
Bram keeps his back to the cooper's stone and lets the wagon come to him.

Wagons are his trade, and at this range he reads it without effort. It's a flat-bed with high sideboards, and the boards are bare: no house colours, no painted name, no Nashkel iron-mark, nothing a merchant would put on his own stock. The harness is plain leather with no brass on it. The big grey cob has feathered hooves and a chest built for heavy hauling, but it walks easily and the axle doesn't groan. The bed rides high on its springs, so it's empty. Somebody hired a strong horse and an empty wagon to collect a load at midnight. The heavy man in the leather hood drives like he's paid by the job, not by the house.

It doesn't turn toward the loading yard. It comes on into the door lantern's fan and stops short of Gorm, who has stepped into the road with the lantern held up. The smaller cloaked figure on the bench leans down toward him, and the hood stays up. Gorm's head turns from the bench to the yard gates and back. Over the hammering Bram can't hear a word of it.

Then, in the gap between one hammer-fall and the next, a small bell rings out across the yard: three quick, tinny strokes from the lodging. After it comes a man's voice, loud enough to cut through the forge: "The high one! That's the high shutter! Up, the lot of you, up!"

Lights come on behind the low wall, one, then another. A door bangs. Within a couple of minutes lanterns are bobbing in the loading yard, four of them, swinging at hip height the way men carry them when they've a cudgel in the other hand. They don't open the plank gates. They spread along the inside of the yard, and the lamplight slides over the canvas on the crates, the barred loading doors and the warehouse's yard wall, working toward the corner where the downpipe runs into the dark.

At the door Gorm calls out slow and loud, "What's that? What's the bell?" The carter hauls the cob back a step, and it stamps and blows. The cloaked figure doesn't sit back. It leans further down from the bench, one gloved hand chopping the air at Gorm, and the wagon stays where it is.

Tobin doesn't go to the yard. He doesn't even look at it. He comes off the doorpost and walks fast down the Coast Way, nearly at a run, out of the lantern light and south toward the bend and the cooper's wall. He's about sixty feet off and coming straight on, his eyes fixed on the dark road past the corner.

presses.text:
Tobin's boots come on fast over the cobbles, and he passes within arm's reach of you. His chest is heaving and he mutters something about the lamp, about being late, but he doesn't look left. His gaze is fixed on the dark road past the bend. He goes round the corner and is gone, his footsteps slapping away south, leaving the cooper's wall and the bend in quiet.

At the warehouse door, Gorm still stands in the road with his lantern, and the wagon with its high sideboards has drawn closer to the yard gates. The driver twists in his seat, short reins gathered in one fist, while the cloaked figure points now toward the yard, now toward the open shutter up the warehouse wall. The grey cob shifts and steams. You cannot hear the words, but you hear their shape: a man's voice raised, a woman's — if it is a woman's — answering low and flat, and Gorm between them, saying no over something.

Inside the yard, four lanterns still move. The men don't climb the wall or throw open a gate; they hold their ground and walk their beat, looking up at the roof line and the shutter. The shutter is closed now. You didn't see it move, but it sits flush with its frame, biting the light. Over the yard the high thin bell had rung only once, three strokes, and since then nothing.

Bram is still at the warehouse door.

Where you are: still in the shadow by the cooper's wall, the bend now empty before you · Time: Day 1 · night

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't think about it. He slides the pick out of the gap and leaves the hook where it is. He doesn't go in. A man inside a dark room with one window and everyone running toward it is a man in a sack.

He goes up instead. He takes the beam-ends above the shutter two at a time, then the eaves, and rolls over onto the roof on the side away from the lodging. The Wide taught him roofs before it taught him locks. He lies flat in the shadow of the ridge or behind a chimney, whichever is nearer, pulls his cloak over the pale of his hands and face, and goes still. (Cunning Action: Hide, if it needs a roll.)

From there he watches, and he takes his time doing it:
- How many come out of the lodging, and what they carry.
- Whether anyone heads for the loading doors with a key, which would tell him who holds keys to this place besides Gorm.
- That wagon on the Coast Way. Who's driving it, which way it came from, and whether Tobin goes to meet it. If skinny's somebody has turned up at the moment the bell rang, Pell wants their faces.

He keeps one ear on the street for Sefa's whistle.

While he lies there, he runs his fingertips along the roof near him, feeling for loose slates, a smoke-hole or a hatch. Someone wired the shutter. That makes him think they never thought much about the roof.

He doesn't move again until the lanterns have stopped looking up.

scenes.narration:
Pell draws the pick out of the gap in one smooth pull and leaves the hook in its eye. Two low whistles come up from the cooper's corner under the hammering. Above him the beam-ends go on up the timber framing to the eaves. He climbs them two at a time, as fast as he'd walk a street, while the lamplight crawls up the yard wall below.

He gets a hand over the eaves and rolls up onto the roof on the street side, away from the lodging, with no scrape at all. A chimney stack stands a few feet up the slope from where he lands. He slides into its shadow, pulls his cloak over his hands and face, and lies still. A moment later lantern light rises over the edge of the roof below him, catches the gutter, and drops back down. Nobody on the ground has seen anything but slate and dark.

From up here the whole night lies open below him.

**The yard.** He counts four lanterns, held at hip height, and four cudgels. One of the men is the one from the window, shirt still untied. The two biggest hold their lamps up to the corner and the downpipe. One of them hits the pipe with his cudgel, the way you'd poke a hedge for a fox, and it rings dully. "Nobody on it," he calls. "Bracket's sprung, look." The window man crosses straight to the barred loading doors. Pell watches his hands. There's no key. The doors are fastened outside with a plain drop-bar in iron staples, and he and a second man lift it out together. That's how it was fastened: a bar anyone in the yard could lift, and a bell on the shutter for anyone who didn't come through the yard. The two of them slip inside with one lantern, and the doors close. A moment later timber thuds against timber on the inside, a bar going home. Whoever has the key to the bright lock on the front, it isn't these men.

The window man's voice comes muffled through the warehouse wall under Pell's chest: "...and somebody get the watch, Hob, go on!" The yard gate's crossbar scrapes. One man slips out through a gap and runs north up the Coast Way, past the wagon, holding his lantern high. The last man stays by the corner with his lamp turned up to the high shutter. He watches it the way a man watches a dog that has growled once.

**The street.** The wagon stands in Gorm's lantern light facing south, so it came down from the north. The carter is a heavy man in a leather hood, holding the cob's head short while it stamps. The figure beside him is small, cloaked, with the hood well forward. Gorm stands at the wheel and looks up, and the figure leans down at him. Pell can't hear a word over the forge, but he can read hands. A gloved hand stabs down toward the yard gates. Then it opens flat, palm down, and presses at the air twice, the way you'd tell a man to keep it quiet. Gorm shakes his head slowly and points north, after the running man. The hand closes into a fist and goes back under the cloak. Pell never sees a face. The hood stays turned toward Gorm, never toward the yard or the roof.

**Skinny.** Tobin never goes to the wagon. He's already well past it, going hard south, nearly running, into the forge-glow and on toward the bend and the cooper's wall. He doesn't look back at the yard or the wagon. Whoever he wants, it isn't anybody in that cart.

**The roof.** Pell lies still and lets his fingers do the looking. The slates are old and furred with soot, and some of the pegs have rotted. Two slates just above his hip lift a hair under his fingertip and settle back with the faintest grit. Lifting a run of them would take care and time, and every one would have to be set down again without a sound. The chimney beside him is cold brick that smells of old soot, the same cold ash he smelled through the shutter gap. Wherever the room under the high shutter is, this stack serves it. The flue is a plain square, too narrow for anything bigger than a cat. He finds no hatch or smoke-hole within reach, and if there's a hoist door on the gable, it's on the far end, out of his sight.

Under the slates, inside the warehouse, boots cross the boards. A door opens and shuts somewhere, and a man's voice says something short that ends in a laugh. They aren't searching the office. They're standing in the dark with a lantern, waiting for the watch.

Below at the corner, the last man lowers his lamp at last and spits in the straw. He stays where he is.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’m going to see who’s collecting a load,” I say quietly to Sefa.

I step out of the shadow, leaving Tobin room to pass without blocking him, and walk briskly back toward Gorm. My sword stays sheathed.

“Gorm! You’ve men shouting about an open shutter and an empty wagon at your door. Is that Oake’s clerk on the bench?”

I look up at the cloaked figure as I approach, trying to get a clear view beneath the hood.

cards.title: Perception: a look under the hood of the figure on the wagon bench, lit from below by Gorm's lantern

screens.Bram Halloway:
You step out of the shadow of the staves and swing wide of Tobin, who stands planted at the bend with his back to the warehouse. You walk north up the Coast Way at a road man's pace, shield on your arm, sword sheathed. The forge's red glow slides off your mail, and then Gorm's yellow lantern light takes its place.

Gorm has turned before you are halfway there. He stands at the wagon's front wheel with the lantern raised and watches you come, the way he'd watch a horse he didn't remember hitching. The carter keeps the cob's head short. You call out your question as you close the distance. The cloaked figure on the bench sits back as soon as your voice carries, and the hood turns a little toward you.

You step into the light and look up under the hood.

scenes.narration:
Bram says it low to Sefa and steps out of the staves' shadow. He swings wide of Tobin, who is planted at the bend with his back to the warehouse, and walks north up the Coast Way at a road man's pace with his shield on his arm and his sword in its sheath. The forge's red spill slides off his mail, then Gorm's yellow lantern light takes over.

Gorm has turned before Bram is halfway there. He's still at the wagon's front wheel with the lantern up, and he watches Bram come the way he'd watch a horse he didn't remember hitching. The carter keeps the cob's head short. The cloaked figure on the bench sits back as soon as Bram's voice carries, and the hood turns a little toward him.

Bram calls his question up the street as he comes, and looks up under the hood as he steps into the light.

The figure is quicker than his eyes. As Bram comes into the light the hood dips and turns aside, toward the dark yard gates, so that Gorm's lantern lights only the cloth: good dark wool, damp at the hem, pulled well forward. Bram sees no face and no hair, only the gloved hand that tugs the hood an inch lower and then rests on the bench rail. Whoever it is has done this before, keeping a face out of lantern light.

A voice comes from under the hood. It's low and even, with the careful vowels of someone who writes for a living, and it's aimed at Gorm, not at Bram. "Mr Hadley. Who is this man?"

Gorm doesn't answer her straight away. He lowers the lantern to chest height and looks at Bram, and the easy road-man warmth from before is gone from his face. He isn't hostile. He's working something out.

"Road man," he says to the bench, without looking round. "Came this evening with the Corl woman's letter. Him and two others." Then, to Bram, slowly: "Is that Oake's clerk." He lets it hang a moment and doesn't answer it. "Funny thing. You and your friends walk off down the street, and not a quarter hour later the bell goes on the high shutter." He looks past Bram's shoulder toward the bend and the cooper's wall, then back. "Where's the other two got to?"

The carter shifts on the bench and keeps his eyes on his horse. The hood stays turned to the yard gates.

Up the Coast Way to the north, past the dark house fronts, Hob's lantern is coming back. It's held high like before, but it isn't alone now. Four or five more lights bob behind it at the same steady height, and boots strike the cobbles together, faint under the forge hammers. They're marching, not running, and they're still a long way off.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds perfectly still, only her eyes moving. She can feel Bram’s presence in the dark behind her, and she gives the smallest shake of her head: not yet. She listens to Tobin’s breathing and the scuff of his boots, and to the lanterns working their way around the yard behind them like a slow tide of light.

She doesn’t whisper. The hammers cover a great deal, but not everything, and they are too close for anything but stillness. Her hand stays on the cord of her beads, thumb against a wooden one, counting the distance between Tobin’s shape and the bend, and how far the light is from the corner of the warehouse.

scenes.narration:
Sefa gives the smallest shake of her head into the dark behind her, and nobody is there to see it. Bram's low words reached her a moment ago, *I'm going to see who's collecting a load*, and by the time her chin moves he is already out of the staves' shadow. He swings wide of Tobin, red forge light on his mail and then the yellow of Gorm's lantern, and walks north up the Coast Way with his sword in its sheath. The shadow beside her is empty now, with only the cold hoop-iron and the smell of new-cut oak.

She stays where she is, still.

The lanterns in the yard have stopped moving. One lamp is left at the downpipe corner, held low, with a man's shape beside it looking up at the high shutter. The other lights have gone inside the warehouse or out through the gate. The yard behind the low wall is darker than it was a minute ago. There is no light on the black timbers by the shutter and nothing moving on them.

Up at the door, Bram steps into the lantern fan beside the wagon. Sefa can't hear a word over the hammers. She sees the hood on the bench turn away from him toward the yard gates. She sees Gorm lower his lantern and face Bram, and then look past Bram's shoulder, down the street, straight at the bend and the cooper's wall. His gaze stays there a moment before it goes back to Bram.

Beyond them, far up the Coast Way to the north, there are lights where there weren't any before. One is held high in front, and four or five more follow it at the same steady height, bobbing together. They are still small with distance, but they are getting bigger.

A few strides south of her, Tobin is still at the bend with his hands on his hips. His breathing has slowed. He hasn't looked back again.

Then running feet slap up the pale road from the last houses. A boy of ten or eleven comes round the bend with a shawl flapping round his shoulders like a cape, and he nearly runs into Tobin.

"Mr Reeve! Mr Reeve, Mam says you're to come. She says *now*, she says don't stop for nothing."

Tobin grabs the boy by both shoulders. "Is she — is it —"

"Mam says *now*," the boy says again, as if that answers everything, and pulls free and starts back the way he came.

Tobin doesn't look at the warehouse, the lanterns or the man standing at his post. He goes after the boy at a dead run, south past the last houses, and the dark takes both of them. For a little while Sefa can still hear his boots. Then there is only the forge, the dog among the yards, and the marching lights coming slowly down the Coast Way from the north.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays exactly where he is. Two whistles means trouble, and he promised Sefa he'd go quiet and stay put, so he does. He keeps his cheek to the cold slate and his breathing slow.

First he watches south. Tobin is running toward the bend, toward the cooper's wall where Sefa is standing. Pell follows him with his eyes the whole way. Does he go past her? Does he stop? Does he meet anyone there? Pell's hand drifts to the shortbow on his back, but he doesn't unsling it. If Tobin lays a hand on her, that changes things. Until then Pell stays a shadow by a chimney.

Second, the hooded figure. Pell fixes what he can on it: height, the cut of the cloak, how it sits, whether it gets down or stays on the wagon, and which way the wagon goes if it leaves. He doesn't need a face to know someone again. A walk and a pair of gloves will do.

Third, the inside. He shifts a hand's width toward the two loose slates by his hip and lays his ear flat against them, close to the chimney stack whose flue runs down to the room with the cold ash. He isn't lifting anything yet. He's listening: how many voices, where they're standing, whether either of them goes near the office door, and whether the laugh was about the bell or about something else. If the men inside talk about who wired the shutter, or who's coming for that office, Pell wants every word.

He doesn't touch the pegs. With the watch on its way and a man spitting in the straw below, a slate sliding off the roof would be the end of the night. If the hammers keep going and the street stays busy, he can start on the slates later. For now he lies still, watches and listens, and counts how long it takes the watch to come.

cards.title: Perception: catching the words of the two men inside, through slate and boards and over the forge

screens.Pell Dunmore:

It dips and turns away from the lantern toward the yard gates, which means more or less toward the roof. Pell can't see any face in it, only the dark mouth of the hood. Seated, the figure's head barely reaches the carter's shoulder. The cloak is long and full, good dark wool with a deep hood and no clasp showing at the throat. The gloves are dark and close-fitting, like a rider's, or a clerk's who writes outdoors. The figure sits very straight with both feet braced on the footboard, like someone who doesn't ride on wagons much and doesn't like it. One gloved hand comes up and tugs the hood an inch lower. As the leather pulls tight over the knuckles, Pell catches a small hard ridge under the glove at the base of the third finger. It could be a ring. The figure doesn't get down. The wagon doesn't move. Gorm has turned to face Bram, lantern lowered, and his stance has changed. It isn't hostile, but he isn't leaning on anything now.

**Under the slates.** Pell eases a hand's width up the slope, keeping close to the chimney stack, and lays his ear flat against the two loose slates. He sorts through the noise the way he would at a keyhole: forge, horse, the hiss of the door lantern, and under all of it the warehouse.

Pell presses his ear to the slate and gets nothing usable. Just then the apprentices bring a fresh piece out of the fire and start on it with the big hammer. Every stroke rings up through the timbers and into the slate under his cheek, so the old roof hums with it. Two voices are down there somewhere, toward the north end of the building and well below him. He can tell there are two because one is higher than the other. He can't pick out a single word. Once, between strokes, one of them barks a laugh and the other answers with a grunt. Then the hammer comes down again and swallows both. As far as he can tell, neither voice moves. Nobody walks toward the room under the chimney.

**North.** The marching lights are a lot closer now. From the roof Pell can count them before anyone in the street could. Hob's lantern is held high at the front, and five more come behind it in a double file at the same height, all in step. Above the lanterns, points of light bob in time with the boots: spearheads, five of them, with the round shine of helmets under them. They're perhaps two hundred feet up the Coast Way and coming on at an even walk with no hurry in it, like men who already know what they'll find.

Below him at the downpipe corner, the last lodging man hears the boots too. He lifts his lamp and turns toward the street, and for the first time since he spat in the straw he isn't looking up at the high shutter.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I left Sefa by the cooper’s wall. Pell can answer for himself,” I say. “I heard the bell from the street, same as you.”

I stop a few paces from Gorm, keeping clear of the horse.

“You told us nobody goes in, and particularly not into the office. Now there’s an empty wagon here and someone keeping her face hidden. Before you put this on us, ask what she’s come to take.”

I look toward the bench. “Bram Halloway. Hesta Corl hired me to collect her deed box. Who are you, and have you authority to remove goods before the court sits?”

scenes.narration:
Gorm hears Bram out with the lantern held at chest height. His face doesn't change at *I heard the bell from the street, same as you*. When Bram turns the question on the wagon, though, Gorm's eyes go to the bench and stay there.

The hood doesn't turn toward Bram. The answer comes from under it in the same low, careful voice, pitched for Gorm as much as for Bram.

"I am Mr Oake's clerk. Mr Oake holds every note on this building, and until the court sits I speak for him. My name is no business of a hired man's." The gloved hand lies still on the bench rail. "As for removing goods, nobody here has talked of removing anything except you."

The carter keeps his eyes on the cob's ears. For a moment, though, the reins go slack in his fists, and he glances sideways at the hood like a man who has just heard his job described as something else.

Gorm says nothing for a long breath. Then, quietly, to the bench: "You asked me to open the yard gates, mistress. Twice." He doesn't look at Bram. "I said no to him and I said no to you. Nothing goes in. And nothing goes out neither, not till the court." He sets his feet a little wider in the road, square between the wagon and the yard. It puts him on nobody's side but Oake's order as he understood it at lamp-lighting.

"Mr Hadley." The voice is still even. "You'll be paid for tonight. Whether you're hired again is another matter."

Gorm doesn't answer that.

The marching boots are loud now even over the forge. Hob comes into the lantern fan first, red in the face and still carrying his lamp high, and five Flaming Fist spearmen come in double file behind him. Their tabards look rust-coloured in the bad light, with the fist badge stitched on the breast, and the helmets are dented and well kept. Last comes a sergeant, a grey-stubbled man of fifty with a short sword on his hip and no spear. He walks past Gorm and Bram as if they were bollards and stops at the wagon's front wheel.

"Mistress," he says, and touches his helmet to the hood. He doesn't ask her name and he doesn't look at the empty wagon bed. "Hob says you've had a bell."

"On the high shutter, Sergeant Tull. Three strokes." She tips her head, an inch, toward Bram. "This man and two others came to the door this evening with the Corl woman's letter. Mr Hadley sent them off. Within the quarter hour the bell rang. The other two have not been seen since."

Gorm opens his mouth and shuts it again. What she said is true as far as it goes, and he plainly knows it.

Sergeant Tull turns and looks Bram up and down by the light of six lanterns: the mail, the shield, the sheathed sword, the road man's boots. He takes his time over it. "Corl letter. That's paper for the magistrate at dawn, not for a warehouse at midnight." He jerks his chin without looking round. "Dace, Pruett, the yard gate. Nobody through it. Hallam, Orrin, take a light down to the bend and find me the other two. A man and a woman." He doesn't say which way he thinks they went. Gorm's look down the street earlier was answer enough, and Hob is already pointing south, toward the forge and the cooper's wall.

Two spearmen break off with a lantern and go south down the Coast Way at a steady walk, their spearheads catching the forge's red glow. Two more go to the plank gates and plant their spear-butts in the dirt on either side. The fifth stays where he is, a long arm's reach from Bram's shoulder, his spear upright and his eyes on Bram's sword hand.

On the bench, the hood turns at last. It isn't turned toward Bram. It's turned toward the yard gates and the two spearmen now standing at them.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays in the black mouth of the stave-stack, listening south until Tobin’s running footsteps are gone. Then she shifts along the wall by inches, toward the corner where the shadow thins, and watches the lights coming down from the north. She straightens slowly, only enough to see between the stacked timbers, and lets her night-eyes work while she counts the lanterns and tries to make out what walks under them.

Her breath stays even. One hand rests at her side, not on the dagger, but close.

scenes.narration:
Tobin's footsteps fade south among the last houses and stop being a sound at all. Sefa waits a few breaths longer to be sure, then edges along the cooper's wall a few inches at a time. The staves press cold against her shoulder. Near the end of the stack the shadow goes grey where the forge's red spill reaches it, and she stops just short of that. She rises only far enough to look out through a gap between two staves.

The lights from the north have reached the door. Hob's lamp is the first she picks out, still held high, and Gorm's lantern is on its hook. She counts five more, and under them helmets and spearheads catch the light. The men wear tabards that look rust-red in this light, with a stitched badge on the breast: the Flaming Fist, five spearmen. A sixth man with them carries no spear and walks past everyone else to stand at the wagon's front wheel. The others give him room. That makes him their sergeant.

Bram is standing in the middle of it all, a few paces from Gorm, his shield on his arm and his sword sheathed. One spearman stands close beside him, an arm's length from his shoulder, and doesn't move.

She can't hear anything over the hammering. She sees the sergeant look Bram up and down, taking his time. Then Hob turns and points with his whole arm down the Coast Way, past the forge, at the bend and the cooper's wall. He's pointing at the stack she's standing behind.

Two spearmen go to the yard's plank gates and plant their spear-butts on either side. Two more take a lantern and come south.

They walk steadily, without hurrying, side by side down the middle of the street, and the lantern swings between them. When they come into the forge's glow their spearheads turn red. The apprentices glance up for the first time all night, then go back to their iron. One spearman lifts the lantern to head height and throws its light ahead of them across the cobbles. It reaches the far house fronts and then the near ones, sweeping from side to side.

In a gap between two hammer-falls, a young voice carries clearly from the nearer of the two: "...man and a woman, he said. By the barrels."

"Staves," the other says. "Cooper's."

They're about forty feet off and coming straight on. The lantern light slides along the base of the cooper's wall, over hoop-iron and the first of the staves, toward the end of the stack where the shadow is already thin.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets out a slow breath against the slate. The hammer drowned the talk, and there's no point cursing it.

When the corner man turns his lamp to the street, Pell moves. He stays below the ridge on the dark slope, hands and toes spread flat to keep his weight off any one slate, and keeps to the line of the roof-timbers where they're less likely to crack. He works along toward the far gable end, the one he couldn't see. He's looking for a hoist door, a beam for a pulley, a loft hatch, anything into the upper floor that isn't wired to a bell. He's also looking for a second way down that doesn't drop into that yard corner, in case he has to leave in a hurry.

Each time he stops, he looks back at the wagon. When the watch's spears come into Gorm's light, what does the hooded figure do? Does the hood duck, does the carter turn the cob, does anyone get down? If the wagon pulls away, Pell marks which way it goes: back north, or on south past the bend after Tobin.

If anyone in the yard starts calling for a ladder, or a lantern comes up the downpipe, he stops wherever he is, flattens into the nearest shadow, and stays there. He doesn't touch the slates. He'll make no noise until the watch has looked at its shutter, found nothing, and got bored.

He also keeps an ear on the cooper's corner, in case Sefa whistles again.

cards.title: Stealth: crossing the old slates to the far gable unheard and unseen, with the Fist's lanterns in the street below

screens.Pell Dunmore:
You let out a slow breath against the slate. The hammer drowned the talk below, and cursing it won't help.

You wait for the corner man's lamp to swing toward the street. When it does, you move.

You keep below the ridge, where the forge glow doesn't reach and the street lanterns light only the gutter. Your hands and toes are spread wide so your weight never rests on one slate, and you feel for the timber running under each course before you lean on it. Here and there a rotted peg shifts under your fingers. You work north along the slope toward the far gable, a few feet at a time, and every few feet you stop and lie flat.

places.Pell Dunmore: on the dark slate slope of the roof, below the ridge, working north toward the far gable

scenes.narration:
Pell waits for the corner man's lamp to swing toward the street. When it does, he moves.

He keeps below the ridge, where the forge glow doesn't reach and the street lanterns light only the gutter. He spreads his hands and toes wide so his weight never rests on one slate, and he feels for the timber running under each course before he leans on it. Rotted pegs shift under his fingers here and there. He works north along the slope toward the far gable, a few feet at a time, and every few feet he stops and lies flat.

Pell crosses the whole roof without a sound. A slate shifts under his left hand halfway along, and he takes his weight off it before it can grate. Nobody in the street looks up, and he reaches the north end with no lamp lifted toward the slates.

**On the way.** Every time he stops he looks back down at the street. The spearmen come into Gorm's light. The hood doesn't duck from them, and nobody on the bench moves. The sergeant walks straight up to the front wheel and touches his helmet to the figure on the bench, as he might to someone he's met before. The carter keeps the cob where it is. No one gets down. Pell sees Hob throw out his arm and point south down the Coast Way toward the forge and the cooper's wall. Two spearmen leave with a lantern and walk that way, side by side, spearheads red in the forge glow. Two others plant themselves at the yard's plank gates. A fifth stays beside Bram, near enough to touch him.

At Pell's next stop the figure on the bench has leaned down toward the sergeant and is talking. Pell can't hear it, but he can read the hood's angle and the stillness of the gloved hand on the bench rail. It's the patient, close talk of someone who has been told no once tonight and is now trying the man above the one who said it. Every so often the hood turns an inch toward the yard gates and the two spears standing there. The wagon doesn't leave.

He listens for the cooper's corner through all of it. No whistle comes. The two spearmen's lantern goes on toward the staves.

**The far gable.** At the north end the roof stops at a gable wall of timber and plaster. Pell hangs his head over the edge and looks.

There is a hoist. An oak beam juts about four feet out from under the peak, with an iron pulley wheel at its end and no rope on it. Below the beam, around twelve feet above the street, is the loft door it serves: two leaves of planking, shut. Pell leans out as far as he dares and looks at where the leaves meet. Through a crack between the planks, the dark inside holds one small, sharp gleam. Pell turns his head so the faint street light strikes it. A thin, straight line runs from the inside of one leaf back into the black, taut, and too clean to be anything old in this building. It's another wire. Whoever wired the high shutter came up here as well, so this door is also a bell. He doesn't touch it.

There is a way down, though, and it isn't the yard. Against the north gable a lower building leans its shoulder on the warehouse. It's a chandler's or a sail-loft, and its roof is shingle, about eight feet below the warehouse eaves and pitched gently toward the next yard over. Past it is a run of back roofs, sheds and a dark lane between the houses, all well away from the Corl yard, the lodging and the lanterns. For a man who learned roofs before locks, it's an open road.

**Below him.** Through the slates under Pell's chest, somewhere near this end, the two men inside are still where they were. One says something, the other answers, and the forge drowns both. Neither has moved toward the south end or the room under the cold chimney.

In the yard nobody has called for a ladder. The corner man has turned his lamp back to the high shutter and stands under it with his cudgel, looking up. Out in the street the hood is still bent toward the sergeant at the wheel, and down at the bend the two spearmen's lantern has reached the cooper's wall.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep my hands still and away from my sword.

“Sergeant, I asked at the door and accepted Gorm’s refusal. I came back openly when the bell rang. I’ll stay here while you look into it.”

I nod toward Gorm. “But keep his whole account: this clerk asked him twice to open the yard gates for this wagon, and threatened his work when he refused. He’s held to his orders. Don’t let him lose his place for telling you so.”

Then I address Tull directly. “Are we being detained, or may we take our claim to Oake?”

scenes.narration:
Bram keeps his hands where everyone can see them and says his piece to Sergeant Tull in a level voice. The spearman at his shoulder doesn't move. His eyes go from Bram's sword hand to Bram's face and back again.

Tull hears it all out without interrupting. When Bram gets to *asked him twice*, the sergeant's head turns, slowly, toward Gorm.

"That so, Hadley?"

"Twice." Gorm doesn't look at the bench. "That's so."

For a moment nobody says anything. The forge rings down the street. The carter studies his cob's ears like a man who wishes he were somewhere else. On the bench the hood doesn't move, but the gloved hand on the rail has closed around it.

"Then you kept your order," Tull says to Gorm. "Good. Now it's mine." He turns back to Bram and looks him over again, the way he did when he arrived, as if the answer were written on his mail. "You're not taken up. You're not walking off either. You stay where Orrin can reach you till my lads come back from the bend with your friends, or without them. Then we'll see." He flicks a glance up the dark street. "And nobody's knocking up a moneylender at midnight over a letter. Your claim waits for the magistrate, same as his."

He jerks his chin toward the yard without looking round. "Dace. Pruett. Open the gates. Wagon goes in off the street. It's blocking the Way." He raises his voice a little, for Gorm and Bram as much as for his men. "Gates shut behind it. Nothing comes out of that yard till the court sits. My word on it."

"Thank you, Sergeant Tull." The clerk's voice is as even as before. "Mr Oake will be glad the yard is secured."

Gorm opens his mouth. Then he looks at the five rust-red tabards and the sergeant's short sword, and he shuts it. He steps back against the doorpost under the lantern. He hasn't stood aside so much as been moved aside, and his face says he knows it. Before he settles, his eyes find Bram's for a moment. It isn't warm, but it isn't the wary look from before either. It's the look one road man gives another when they've both watched the boss make a bad call.

Dace and Pruett lift the crossbar off the plank gates. The greased hinges don't make a sound. The carter clicks his tongue, the big grey cob leans into the collar, and the empty wagon turns off the Coast Way and rolls into the yard with its iron tyres crunching on the straw. The hood never turns to look back. The gates swing shut behind it and the bar drops into place. Dace and Pruett plant their spear-butts again, outside the gates now, facing the street.

Over the low wall, lantern light moves in the yard. Someone calls a short question, and the corner man answers it. Then Bram hears a sound he knows from a hundred loading yards: the dull knock of a brick dropped on beaten earth, then another, then a third. They're taking the weights off the canvas.

Down at the bend the patrol's lantern has stopped at the cooper's wall. From here Bram can see only the light, held head-high at the stacked staves, and two spearheads catching the forge's red glow beside it.

messages.text:
Sefa watches the light come toward her along the stave-stack, then touches the beads once and steps deliberately out of the shadow before it can reach her. She keeps her hands open and low, chin up, as though she’d been walking south along the wall and only now thought to show herself.

“There’s no need for all that,” she says, calm enough to carry to the nearer spearman. “I’m the woman from the warehouse—” She doesn’t finish the thought, instead trusting the words to land as if she were known. “I only came back this way because the road ahead is darker than I like.”

presses.text:
The one with the lantern, the nearer of the two, is young and clean-shaven under his helmet. His eyes are red-rimmed from the forge smoke, and he blinks hard when you step into the light, as if he'd half expected no one to be there. The other lowers his spear a hand's width, not at you, just ready, and plants his feet.

"Turned back from the dark road," the young one echoes flatly. "With the Fist fetching you from the barrels to the staves." He takes in your studded garb, your hands, the beads. "I don't know your face."

The lantern light fills the space between you. The other man has a hard, pock-marked face and the look of someone who has stood in a lot of doorways. He hooks a thumb over his shoulder without taking his eyes off you. "She'll come over to the sergeant," he says. "He can take her name. If he thinks she's the one he's after, that's his to say."

The younger one steps aside and lifts the lantern so you can pass between them. "Best come, then. We won't drag you." There is no shout, no spearpoint raised, but there is also no room in the road to run. Behind them the bend is at your back and the dark is fading forward, and a few strides behind them the firelight and the empty forge bay make a wall of red along one side of the street. Past that lie Gorm's lantern and the sergeant still waiting by the wagon.

The hammers have fallen quiet at last. In the hush, you hear your boots on the cobbles and the phlegmy rasp of the pock-marked man's breathing. From somewhere down the road, very faint, a boy's voice is calling for Mr Reeve, receding.

Where you are: stepping out of the staves' shadow at the Coast Way bend, the two spearmen a couple of strides off, light and spear flanking a path back toward the warehouse · Time: Day 1 · night

scenes.narration:
Sefa touches the beads once and steps out of the shadow before the lantern finds her. She keeps her hands open and low and her chin up, and walks into the light along the wall like a woman who has been going somewhere.

The lantern jerks up to her face. Both spearheads come down a hand's breadth. They don't level at her, but they stop pointing at the sky.

She says it calmly, loud enough to reach the nearer man. For a breath the cracked bead under her thumb is warm, like lamp-glass just after the flame goes out. Then it's only wood again.

It doesn't work, and the hole is in the story itself. The nearer spearman is young, with a soft jaw under a dented helmet. He holds the lantern and looks from her to the staves and back. He watched the light slide along that wall, and he watched her come out of the dark at the end of it, not down the road.

"Came back from where?" he says. "You come out of them staves, mistress. I seen you."

The older one beside him is lean and pocked, with a spear held easily in one hand. He doesn't bother answering her. He looks past her shoulder into the stave-shadow she just left. "The woman from the warehouse," he repeats, as if he's writing it down. "That's what Hob said. Man and a woman, gone off down here, and then the bell." He jerks his head at the young one. "Look in the stack, Pell's our man is tall, he'll—" He stops, frowns, and starts again. "Look for the man. Hallam's going nowhere till you do."

The young one gives the lantern to Hallam and walks the length of the staves. He jabs his spear-butt into the gaps and kicks the hoop-iron so it rings. At the far end he leans round the corner of the cooper's wall and looks at the bend and the empty pale road south. He comes back shaking his head. "Nobody. Just her."

"Then she'll do for now." Hallam gives Sefa a look without much in it, the look of a man who was sent to fetch something and has found half of it. "Sergeant wants a word with you at the door. You walk in front, hands where I can see them. You've got a knife there. Leave it be."

They don't take hold of her. The young one falls in on her left and Hallam on her right, half a step behind, with the lantern held up so it lights her back. The three of them turn north up the Coast Way, into the forge's red spill and out of it. Up ahead Gorm's lantern burns on its hook by the warehouse door. Men stand around it: spears, the sergeant's grey head, and a broad shape in mail. Behind the low wall of the yard, lantern light moves, and something heavy thumps onto a wagon bed.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell leaves the hoist door alone. Two wires in one night means the whole place is strung like a harp, and he isn't going to pluck it with the Fist standing in the street.

He lowers himself off the north eaves by his fingertips. He picks a spot where the chandler's roof has a rafter under it, not the middle of a run of shingles, and lets himself down the last couple of feet so he lands soft and low. Then he goes flat on the shingle, below the line of the warehouse eaves, where neither the yard nor the street can see him. Now he has a way out that doesn't pass a single lantern.

From there he edges to where he can look down the Coast Way toward the cooper's wall, and he watches the two spearmen reach Sefa. That's her game to play. A hospice novice out late is no crime, and he has the letter, not her. He wants to see how it goes: whether they bring her back to the wagon, and whether the hood turns to look at her when they do. If they march her off anywhere but the street in front of the warehouse, he'll follow over the back roofs.

He keeps track of three other things while he watches. One is whether the sergeant gives the hooded one what it's asking for, so whether the spears at the gate step aside and anyone goes into the yard with a key. Another is whether the two men inside ever walk south toward the office end. The last is how long the Fist means to stay.

Lying there, he plans the next attempt in his head. The two loose slates by the cold chimney sit right over Anvar's office. Nobody wires a roof. Once the street goes quiet and the spears have gone home, he can go back up the way he came down and lift a run of slates one at a time.

scenes.narration:
Pell lets the hoist door be. He goes back along the gable to the street-side corner of the eaves, hooks his fingers over the gutter and lowers himself until he's hanging at full stretch. Under his boots he feels for where the chandler's roof would have a rafter. He finds the line where the shingles sit a little higher and harder and drops the last couple of feet onto it. He lands bent-kneed and low. The shingle flexes and holds, and the forge's hammering covers the small knock of his heels. Then he lies flat with the warehouse eaves an arm's length above him and the shingle still warm from the day. Down here he's below every lantern in the street and has a way out at his back.

While he was hanging from the gutter he heard iron tyres crunch and the big cob blow. When he edges to the street side of the chandler's roof and looks south down the Coast Way, the wagon is gone. Its spot in Gorm's lantern light is empty cobbles. The yard's plank gates are shut, and two spearmen stand outside them with their spear-butts in the dirt, facing the street. From this end the warehouse hides the yard completely, but a glow rises over its south end where there was only dark a few minutes ago. More than one lantern is burning in there. He can't see the hood or the carter, so whatever they're doing, they're doing it inside the low wall.

At the door Bram stands in the lantern fan with a spearman close at his shoulder, and Gorm leans against the doorpost again. The grey-stubbled sergeant stands a little apart with his thumbs in his belt, the way a man stands when he plans to be there a while. Nobody in the street looks like they're leaving.

South along the Coast Way, a lantern comes out of the forge's red spill, held head-high, with two spearheads beside it. A slight figure walks a step ahead of it with her hands out from her sides where they can be seen. At this distance it's Sefa by her walk. Nobody has a hand on her. They don't turn off toward the yard gates or into any side lane. They walk her straight up the middle of the street toward the door and the sergeant, and the light in the yard behind the low wall doesn't change as they pass it.

Under him, the plaster of the north gable carries something to his cheek that the slates didn't. Boots cross the warehouse floor from this end, two pairs, unhurried. They go away from him, south, until the forge swallows them. A while later a single dull wooden thud comes through the wall, far off at the other end of the building. It could be a bar being lifted, or a crate set down. From here Pell has no way of telling which, or which room it came from.

The hammers ring on. The two spears stand at the gate, the sergeant waits at the door, and the glow over the yard stays lit.

 (Out of game: none of the four needed a roll. 1) Dropping eight feet onto a rafter line with the forge covering the sound is routine work for a roof-runner with Second-Story Work, and nobody was watching. 2–3) Watching lit figures in an open street with nothing hiding them works on his passive Perception. 4) Planning the slates is only intent so far, so the roll comes when he actually lifts them.)

scenes.narration:
Bram says it plainly, loud enough to carry over the forge, and keeps his hands where they were. Then he turns his head an inch toward the low wall and listens.

The yard keeps its secrets. Just as Bram turns his ear to it, the apprentices pull a fresh bar out of the fire and set both hammers going on it, one after the other, so the forge rings like a bell-tower. Every word behind the low wall gets lost in it. Bram can make out lantern light sliding across the top of the wall, and once, between two strokes, the hollow knock of something heavy set down on planking. He can't tell if it was a crate going onto the wagon bed or a crate coming off the stack. He hears no voices clearly enough to say who's talking.

Sergeant Tull doesn't look at the yard. He keeps his eyes on Bram and lets the question sit a breath longer than it needs.

"My men stand where I put them," he says. "Two spears on a barred gate. That's witness enough for the magistrate, and it'll do for you." He hooks a thumb back over his shoulder without turning. "The mistress is setting the stock in order for the court's count. Off the wet ground, onto boards. A crate on a wagon bed's the same crate it was on the straw. The court counts it either way."

Gorm moves off the doorpost. He doesn't come far, just a step into the lantern fan, and he speaks to Tull rather than to Bram, slow and careful, like a man setting down something he might be asked to pick up again later.

"I could stand in the yard, Sergeant. I'm Oake's man. If anything goes short at the count, it's me they'll ask."

"You've a door, Hadley." Tull doesn't raise his voice. "Mind it."

Gorm looks at him a moment longer. Then he steps back to the doorpost and stays there, but he doesn't lean on it this time. He stands upright beside the bright new lock with his arms at his sides and his face turned toward the yard gates.

Orrin, the spearman at Bram's shoulder, shifts his grip on his spear. For half a heartbeat his eyes go to the sergeant's back and come away again. It's how a man looks when he's heard an order he wouldn't have given himself and won't say so.

Out at the gates Dace and Pruett face the street and stand like posts. The lantern glow over the yard brightens, dims as someone carries a light past the wall, and brightens again. Down at the bend the search lantern has left the cooper's staves and is moving north up the middle of the Coast Way, held head-high.

messages.text:
Sefa walks with her head up and her hands held a little away from her sides, making no move toward the dagger. The forge glow slides over her as she passes, then leaves her in the dark between one lantern and the next.

scenes.narration:
Sefa walks up the middle of the Coast Way with her hands held a little out from her sides. Hallam's lantern is behind her, so her own shadow goes ahead of her on the cobbles, long and thin, shrinking each time he lifts the light. The forge's red glow slides over her and off her again. One apprentice looks up from the anvil as the three of them pass, sees the spears and looks down at his iron.

Neither spearman speaks to her. The young one keeps half a pace off her left shoulder, close enough to grab her and not touching her. Twice she hears him breathe in as if he means to say something, and both times he lets it go.

The warehouse corner comes up on her right. Past it, where the downpipe runs down into the dark, the low yard wall begins. Over its top the lantern glow is bright and uneven, many lights moving, and nothing stands at the corner or under the high shutter that she can see from the street. Black timber, black iron, and the shutter open its finger's width, exactly as before.

They walk right along the plank gates. Dace and Pruett stand either side of them like posts. Dace gives Hallam a short nod, and Hallam doesn't return it. Up this close the forge noise thins a little, and in the gap between two hammer strokes Sefa hears the yard through the planks. Iron tyres shift on straw. The big cob blows. A man's voice comes, rough and aggrieved, pitched low the way a hired man talks when he wants to be heard without seeming to complain:

"...you said six, mistress. That's nine on the bed and the springs are near flat—"

The hammer comes down, and the rest is lost. Something heavy knocks onto planking. Then they're past the gates.

Ahead, Gorm's lantern burns on its hook beside the bright new lock, and the figures she has been picking out take shape. A grey-headed man stands a little apart with his thumbs in his belt. He has no spear, only a short sword on his hip. A spearman stands upright at a broad shoulder in mail. Gorm stands beside the door. He isn't leaning on the post now; he's standing straight with his arms at his sides.

Hallam lengthens his stride to pass her the last few feet and steps into the light first.

"Sergeant. The woman. She was in the cooper's staves, hiding. No sign of the man. We went down to the bend and past it."

The grey-headed man turns. He doesn't hurry it. He looks at her by the light of Gorm's lantern and Hallam's together, from her face to her open hands, to the dagger at her hip, to the beads at her wrist, and back to her face. Behind him the glow over the yard wall flares brighter as someone carries a lamp close to the boards, then falls back.
