messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't like it. The wagon is in the yard, the lanterns are lit at the south end, and two pairs of boots just walked toward the office. Whoever was told no once tonight has found someone who said yes.

He can't do anything for Sefa from a roof, and he trusts her to play the lost novice. So he goes back up. He reaches for the warehouse gutter, finds the beam-ends under the gable corner, and is over the eaves and flat on the dark street-side slope in a few breaths. Then he works south the way he came, on the same timber lines, testing each hold, past the slate that shifted last time, until he's back in the shadow of the cold chimney over the office.

There he does two things, slowly.

First, he eases up to the ridge right beside the chimney stack, so the brick breaks his outline, and puts one eye over it, just enough to look down into the yard. He wants the wagon: where it stands, whether the loading doors are open, and who is carrying what. Most of all he wants to know whether an iron box, or anything box-sized, is going onto that wagon, and whether the hood gets down to watch it or stays on the bench. If anyone looks up at the roof, he sinks back below the ridge and doesn't move.

Second, if the voices and lantern light are in the room right under him, he puts his ear back to the two loose slates by the chimney. The forge is louder at this end, but men in a small room with a lantern talk closer. Names, "Oake," "the box," "the key," anything.

He doesn't lift a slate and he doesn't go in. If the wagon is loading up to leave, he'll follow it over the back roofs and the dark lane. He wants to see where it goes, not start a fight with six Fist spears and four cudgels between him and the street.

cards.title: Stealth: looking over the ridge by the chimney into a yard full of lanterns without being seen

screens.Pell Dunmore:
You slide back off the chandler's shingle to the gable corner and find the beam-end under the eaves by feel. You hook the gutter and haul yourself up the eight feet of timber you climbed once already tonight. Before the forge has struck ten times you are over the edge and onto the dark slates. You work south the way you came, one timber line at a time, spreading your weight and testing each hold. When you reach the slate that shifted on the way north, you step over it. The chimney stack takes shape against the sky ahead of you, black against slightly lighter black, and you settle into its shadow.

The yard is brighter now. A wash of lantern light comes up past the south eaves and turns the soot on the slates a dirty gold. To look down into the yard you will have to put your head over the ridge, into that glow.

scenes.narration:
Pell slides back off the chandler's shingle to the gable corner. He finds the beam-end under the eaves by feel, hooks the gutter and pulls himself up. It's eight feet of timber he climbed once already tonight, and he's back over the edge onto the dark slates before the forge has struck ten times. He goes south the way he came, one timber line at a time, spreading his weight. When he reaches the slate that shifted on the way north, he steps over it. The chimney stack takes shape against the sky ahead of him, black against slightly lighter black, and he settles into its shadow.

The yard is brighter now. A wash of lantern light comes up past the south eaves and turns the soot on the slates a dirty gold. To look down into it he has to put his head over the ridge, into that glow.

He brings one eye over the ridge with the brick of the stack beside his cheek and holds still. Nobody below looks up. The light makes them look down, at their hands and feet and the crates. To anyone in that yard the roof is a black edge above the lamps, and the chimney has just grown a little wider on one side.

**The yard.** The wagon stands close against the warehouse's loading doors with its tail to them. The doors are open wide and lantern light spills out of them. The cob has been backed in and hitched short to a ring in the wall, and the carter stands at its head with one hand on its nose. The bed is full. Pell counts the crates the way he'd count guards on a door: three rows of three, nine in all, roped down. The springs sit so low the sideboards almost touch the wheel rims. The canvas that covered the stack is folded on the straw, the bricks beside it in a neat line. Where the crates stood there's a pale square of dry earth and nothing else.

Two lodging men stand by the tail with their cudgels stuck in their belts. They're doing nothing, and they look like they've been told to do nothing. The bench is empty. The hood isn't on the wagon or anywhere in the yard. Nobody is carrying anything iron or box-sized. Whatever is coming out of the building hasn't come out yet.

He sinks back below the ridge into the stack's shadow, turns his head and lays his ear on the two loose slates.

The forge is louder at this end and rings through the old roof the way it did before. This time there's a lantern lit somewhere under him, close, and close voices carry. He catches them between the hammer-strokes.

A man's voice comes first. It's low and comfortable, with flattened Lower City vowels that Pell knows like his own feet, the voice of the Wide. "...heavy for a little thing. Give us the light, I'll have a go at the lock, save carrying it—"

Under the voices Pell hears another sound, and he can't place it at first. It's small and dry, *tick... tick... tick*, like a cooling stove or a beetle in old timber. When the man says *lock* it comes faster.

The woman's voice cuts in, low and even, every vowel careful. "Don't touch the lock." There's a pause, and something scrapes on boards. The ticking falters, then stops dead, as if a hand had been laid on it. "It rides on the bench, with me. Not on the bed with the rest. And we're through the gate before anybody at the court is awake to count anything."

messages.text:
“Understood. I’ll tell the magistrate what I saw, and leave the counting to him.”

I leave it there rather than argue with Tull. Keeping my hands clear and staying within Orrin’s reach, I turn to watch the returning patrol—looking to see whether Sefa or Pell is with them.

If Gorm is close enough to speak without moving away, I ask quietly, “You know the clerk’s name?”

scenes.narration:
Tull hears Bram out and gives him a short nod, the way a man takes something he expected to win. "Do that," he says, and turns away to the street.

Bram leaves it there. He keeps his hands clear and his feet where they are, with Orrin's spear upright an arm's length from his shoulder, and watches the search lantern come up the middle of the Coast Way out of the forge's red spill.

It's two spearmen and one lantern, with Sefa a step ahead of it, her hands held out from her sides. Nobody has hold of her. Bram looks past them down the road, then along the dark house fronts on both sides, and finds nobody else. There's no fourth shape at the edge of the light and nobody walking behind. Pell isn't with them. Hallam steps into the fan of Gorm's lantern and makes his report to the sergeant, short and flat: the woman was in the cooper's staves, hiding, and there was no sign of the man. Tull turns to look Sefa over.

Gorm is only a few paces off, upright at the doorpost. Bram doesn't move toward him. He speaks low, under the hammering.

Gorm doesn't turn his head. He keeps watching the yard gates. "Her name." He thinks about it longer than the question needs, like a man deciding what he owes and to whom. "Venn. Mr Oake calls her Venn. Never heard no front to it." A pause. "She ain't been with him long. Since after the thaw. Before that it was old Pelham kept his books, and Pelham never come out at night for nothing."

Orrin, at Bram's shoulder, is close enough to have heard every word. His eyes stay on Bram's sword hand, and he says nothing.

Behind the low wall the glow over the yard shifts and settles closer to the loading doors. Between two hammer-falls Bram hears a sound he's heard at the start of a thousand mornings: iron rattling on iron, a tether ring knocking against a wall staple as a lead rope comes off it, and then the big cob shaking itself in its harness so every buckle jingles. Gorm hears it too. His jaw sets, and he keeps his eyes on the gates.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text: Sefa lets her eyes meet the sergeant’s without challenge, then lowers them, like a woman tired of standing in the dark. “I did hide,” she says, plainly enough for the men around her to hear. “I’m not a fool. Two guards at the warehouse, one of them watching the road like his life depended on it; the letter is ours, but a letter doesn’t stop a man swinging a cudgel.” She dips her head toward the bright lock and the wall. “Then the bell rang and the Fist came, and I was too far from the three of us by then not to lie about it.” She holds her hands level, open, and lets them fall a little. “I’m not here to trouble your watch, sergeant. I’m hired to carry a box for Hesta Corl before dawn.”

scenes.narration:
Sergeant Tull hears her out without moving. His thumbs stay hooked in his belt. When she lowers her eyes he goes on looking at her face anyway, like a man who doesn't take much from where someone looks.

"You hid," he says. "Then you lied to my man about it. Now you've told me straight." He weighs that for a moment. "That's one in three. I've had worse nights."

Hallam stands at her right shoulder with the lantern held low now. "Too far off not to lie," he says flatly, to nobody in particular.

"Hired to carry a box." Tull's mouth hardly moves. "Then hear it plain, mistress. Whatever Hesta Corl's paper says, it says it to the magistrate at dawn. Till then nobody carries anything out of this building. Not for her, not for anybody." He tips his head a fraction toward the bright lock and lets it drop. "And the man you came with, the quiet one. Where's he got to?"

Behind her the young spearman shifts his feet. Walking her up the street, he passed the plank gates at the same moment she did. When the sergeant says *nobody carries anything*, his eyes go to the gates, to the lantern glow over the low wall and to Dace and Pruett standing like posts, and then come back to the cobbles. He doesn't open his mouth.

Gorm stands upright at the doorpost and says nothing. He heard *a box*, though, and his eyes leave the gates for a moment and rest on Sefa. It's a long, slow look, the look of a man adding up a sum he hasn't liked since lamp-lighting.

Tull points at a spot on the cobbles beside the doorpost, an arm's length from Gorm and squarely in the lantern light. "You stand there. Hands where they are. Hallam, she's yours."

Hallam moves her the two steps with the lantern, not with his hand, and plants himself half a pace off her shoulder.

Down the street the forge apprentices put the iron back in the fire to heat, and for a few breaths the hammers stop. In that gap the yard behind the low wall can be heard. The wagon's springs groan once at the front end, the way a bench groans when something heavy is set on it, not on the bed. A woman's low, even voice says two words Sefa can't make out. The big cob blows and stamps. Then the hammers start again and cover all of it, and the lantern glow over the wall drifts slowly from the loading doors toward the gates.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays where he is a moment longer. The ticking is what bothers him. A box that ticks faster when someone says *lock* isn't a deed box, or it isn't only one. And a woman who won't let it ride on the bed has her own reasons.

He rolls back to the ridge beside the chimney and puts one eye over it again. He waits for the box to come out of the loading doors. He wants to see it: how big it is, how it's carried, whether the Wide man is sweating under it. Most of all he wants the woman when she steps into the lantern light. If the hood is down, he wants her face. If it isn't, he wants her height, her walk, and that ring under the glove. He also wants to see where the box ends up on the bench and how she sits with it, at her feet or on her lap, and whether her hand is on it.

Once he's seen that, he goes. He takes the same timber lines north, quick now and careless of nothing, and drops down to the chandler's shingle. Then he goes across the back roofs, into the dark lane, and comes out onto the Coast Way well north of the lanterns. From there he walks back down the street openly, hood back, hands empty, like a man who went off to find Smithy Row and is now coming back to collect his friends.

If he can get near Bram or Sefa without the sergeant crowding him, he says it low and quick, the way you'd pass a message in the Wide:

"They've got it. It's coming out the yard on the bench, with a woman in a hood. Sergeant's been bought. And the box *ticks*. Don't let anybody pick at its lock. They're going south through the gate before dawn. Heavy wagon, nine crates, a slow cob. We don't fight six spears here. We follow, and we take it where nobody's watching."

If he can't get to them without being noticed, he doesn't force it. He drifts back south along the dark house fronts toward the cooper's bend, the way the wagon has to go, and waits there in the stave-shadow for it to roll past.

cards.title: Stealth: slipping south along the dark house fronts, past the Fist's ring of lanterns at the warehouse door

screens.Pell Dunmore:
You hold still in the chimney's shadow until the stair below stops creaking. Then you ease back up to the ridge, keep the brick against your cheek, and put one eye over the top.

The box comes out of the loading doors first. The Wide-voiced man has one end and a second lodger the other, and they carry it between them on a looped rope, walking short and bowed like men under real weight. It is smaller than its weight: iron, black in the lantern light, about a forearm long and a foot high. Set into the middle of its lid is a round, dull grey disc the size of a palm. Every other bit of metal in the yard throws back some light, from the cob's buckles to the wagon's tyre-iron, but the disc stays flat and grey. The Wide man is broad and thinning on top. His shirt is soaked dark between the shoulders, and when they lift the box onto the bench he blows out his cheeks and wipes both hands down his thighs.

The clerk comes out after it. From above she is the crown of a hood and the fall of a long dark cloak, nothing more. She walks with short, quick steps and her eyes on the straw, and she never looks up. At the front wheel the carter holds out a hand to help her up. She doesn't take it. She climbs on her own, slowly, a foot on the hub and then a hand on the rail, like someone who has had to learn it. She sits down hard against the rail with the box at her right hip, not at her feet. Then she lays one gloved hand flat on the lid, right over the grey disc, and leaves it there.

The carter unhitches the cob from the wall ring. You have what you came up for, and you sink below the ridge.

You go north fast, on the timber lines you have already crossed twice tonight, and step over the slate that shifted without looking down at it. Behind you the gold glow over the yard slides away from the loading doors toward the gates. You drop over the north eaves, find the rafter line on the chandler's shingle with your heels, and keep moving. You cross a shed roof and the top of a privy wall, then let yourself down into the lane, where a washing line catches at your hood and a cat watches you from a water butt. A couple of minutes later you walk out of the lane onto the Coast Way about a hundred and fifty feet north of the warehouse door, hood back, hands empty.

From here the street ahead is a ring of light with no gap in it. Gorm's lantern hangs on its hook, Hallam's is held low, and Hob's lamp is up beside them. Sergeant Tull stands in the middle with his thumbs in his belt. Bram is in the ring with Orrin's spear at his shoulder. Sefa stands at the doorpost with Hallam half a pace off her, and the young spearman behind her. Gorm stands upright beside the lock. Anyone who walks into that light is the quiet man the sergeant has been asking after, and there is no reaching Bram or Sefa without six men watching you do it.

So you don't try. You cross to the far side of the street, where the house fronts are dark and shuttered, and start south along them, unhurried.

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Pell Dunmore's screen continues from where you crossed to the dark side of the street and started south.

You get past them without being seen. You keep a doorstep's width from the walls and walk like a man who lives on the street and isn't hurrying anywhere. Where a doorway is deep you go through its shadow. Where a shutter shows a crack of candlelight you go under it bent at the waist. Across the street the Fist's lanterns throw their light out over the cobbles, and it dies a few feet short of your boots. Nobody in the ring turns your way. Hob's lamp swings once in your direction as he shifts his feet, then swings back toward the sergeant.

You come level with the yard gates. Dace and Pruett stand at them like posts with their backs to the planks, watching the middle of the street. Over the low wall the light has changed. A minute ago the yard was gold with lanterns. Now it shows only one lamp, shuttered down to a slit, close behind the gates. In a gap between hammer-strokes you hear the cob shift its feet on straw and a bit-chain clink, just on the other side of the planks. The wagon is right up against the gates, loaded and hitched, and it isn't moving. Someone in there has put the lights out and settled down to wait.

You go on. The forge's red spill crosses the street ahead of you. One apprentice glances up at a man going past in the dark, shows no interest, and looks back at his iron. Past the forge you cross to the cooper's wall and slide in among the staves, into the deep black where Sefa stood an hour ago. The hoop-iron is cold against your shoulder. From here you can see the bend, the empty pale road running south between the last houses, the lantern ring at the warehouse door, and the dark shut gates with one slit of light behind them.

Pell Dunmore: Pell stays where he is a moment longer. The ticking is what bothers him. A box that ticks faster when someone says *lock* isn't a deed box, or it isn't only one. And a woman who won't let it ride on the bed has her own reasons.

He rolls back to the ridge beside the chimney and puts one eye over it again. He waits for the box to come out of the loading doors. He wants to see it: how big it is, how it's carried, whether the Wide man is sweating under it. Most of all he wants the woman when she steps into the lantern light. If the hood is down, he wants her face. If it isn't, he wants her height, her walk, and that ring under the glove. He also wants to see where the box ends up on the bench and how she sits with it, at her feet or on her lap, and whether her hand is on it.

Once he's seen that, he goes. He takes the same timber lines north, quick now and careless of nothing, and drops down to the chandler's shingle. Then he goes across the back roofs, into the dark lane, and comes out onto the Coast Way well north of the lanterns. From there he walks back down the street openly, hood back, hands empty, like a man who went off to find Smithy Row and is now coming back to collect his friends.

If he can get near Bram or Sefa without the sergeant crowding him, he says it low and quick, the way you'd pass a message in the Wide:

"They've got it. It's coming out the yard on the bench, with a woman in a hood. Sergeant's been bought. And the box *ticks*. Don't let anybody pick at its lock. They're going south through the gate before dawn. Heavy wagon, nine crates, a slow cob. We don't fight six spears here. We follow, and we take it where nobody's watching."

It's smaller than its weight: iron, black in the lantern light, about the length of a man's forearm and a foot high. Set into the middle of its lid is a round, dull grey disc the size of a palm. Every other bit of metal in the yard throws back some light, from the cob's buckles to the wagon's tyre-iron, but the disc stays flat and grey. The Wide man is broad and going thin on top. His shirt is soaked dark between the shoulders, and when they lift the box onto the bench he blows out his cheeks and wipes both hands down his thighs.

The clerk comes out after it. From above she's the crown of a hood and the fall of a long dark cloak, and nothing more. She walks with short, quick steps and her eyes on the straw, and she never looks up. At the front wheel the carter holds out a hand to help her up. She doesn't take it. She climbs on her own, slowly, a foot on the hub and then a hand on the rail, like someone who has had to learn it. She sits down hard against the rail with the box at her right hip, not at her feet. Then she lays one gloved hand flat on the lid, right over the grey disc, and leaves it there.

The carter unhitches the cob from the wall ring. Pell has what he came up for, and he sinks below the ridge.

scenes.narration:
Bram gives Sefa a small nod and turns to Tull without moving from his spot. He says it plainly, loud enough to carry over the forge. His hands stay clear and his eyes stay on the yard gates.

Tull doesn't look at the gates. He looks at Bram for a long moment, and his patience runs out the way a man's does when he's heard one voice too many in a night.

"The driver stays where I put him. So do you, till I say otherwise." He hooks his thumbs back in his belt. "And I'm saying otherwise. You've given me the magistrate, the witness and the horse. That's three times you've told me my business." He speaks to the spearman at Bram's shoulder without turning his head. "Orrin. Walk him up to the post. He can sit on the bench there till the court's awake and tell them all about it."

Orrin doesn't move straight away. His spear stays upright. "Now, Sergeant? That leaves the door one short."

"Hadley's on the door. Now."

Orrin breathes out through his nose. He takes his left hand off the spear shaft and opens it toward the north, up the Coast Way, past Hob and his lamp and on into the dark between the house fronts. He doesn't take hold of Bram. "This way, road man." He says it quietly, with no edge in it, the way you'd tell a carter the bridge is out.

Gorm stands upright beside the bright lock. When Tull says *Hadley's on the door* his head turns, slowly, to the sergeant and then to the plank gates, and Bram sees him work it out. With Bram gone up the Way, Gorm is the only one at that door who doesn't take orders from Tull. He doesn't say anything. He scratches his jaw once, hard, and leaves his hand there.

Behind the low wall the slit of light has gone out. In the gap between two hammer-strokes Bram hears the cob shift on the straw, the bit-chain clink, and wood creak as somebody leans on the inside of the gates, close to the planks, waiting.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stands where she’s placed, near the doorpost under the hanging lantern, and keeps her hands loose and easy. She makes no reply to the sergeant now that he has said his piece. A little of the stiffness leaves her shoulders, the way it does when there’s nothing more to fight for a while.

Her eyes move without turning her head: over the gates, the lamp-light beyond them, the spearmen, and then, slowly, back to the street. She listens under the ring of the hammers, half her attention always on the seam between the lamplight and the dark at the corner of the warehouse, in case a shape breaks from the wall and runs. The bead sits cool at her wrist now, like all the others.

When she speaks, it is only to Gorm, low enough not to reach the sergeant: “That gate has been waiting all evening for the wagon it’s getting.” She doesn’t ask it as a question, only says it the way a man might remark on bad weather, but her gaze levels with his a moment too long.

opening.narration:
The Coast Way smells of coal smoke and hot iron, and the ring of Beregost's hammers never quite stops. Ahead stands the Corl warehouse, its broad door fastened with a heavy new lock that is still bright. Two men lean beside it in the creditors' service. One is a broad, patient fellow with a cudgel at his belt. The other is thinner and keeps glancing up and down the street as if he expects someone.

Pell Dunmore has Hesta Corl's letter of claim, or the three of you share it, along with her promise of 60 gold once the iron deed box reaches her hands. Bram Halloway's chain mail and shield draw the thin guard's eye at once. Sefa Marrin's quiet bearing earns a second look from the broad one. Somewhere inside is Anvar Corl's office, and in it, if all is as Hesta says, the box. Nightfall is the deadline, and at dawn the creditors' court sits.

High on the warehouse wall, one shutter hangs a finger's width open where every other is shut fast. The broad guard pushes himself off the wall and looks the three of you over. "Warehouse is closed by order of the creditors," he says. "You've business here?"

screens.text:
The session begins.

The Coast Way smells of coal smoke and hot iron, and the ring of Beregost's hammers never quite stops. Ahead stands the Corl warehouse, its broad door fastened with a heavy new lock that is still bright. Two men lean beside it in the creditors' service. One is a broad, patient fellow with a cudgel at his belt. The other is thinner and keeps glancing up and down the street as if he expects someone.

Pell Dunmore carries Hesta Corl's letter of claim, which the three of you share, along with her promise of 60 gold once the iron deed box reaches her hands. Your chain mail and shield draw the thin guard's eye at once. Sefa Marrin's quiet bearing earns a second look from the broad one. Somewhere inside is Anvar Corl's office, and in it, if all is as Hesta says, the box. Nightfall is the deadline, and at dawn the creditors' court sits.

High on the warehouse wall, one shutter hangs a finger's width open where every other is shut fast. The broad guard pushes himself off the wall and looks the three of you over. "Warehouse is closed by order of the creditors," he says. "You've business here?"

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: Coast Way, before the Corl warehouse door · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Pell stays half a step behind you, hands loose and empty, and lets you speak first. Then he draws Hesta Corl's letter from inside his jerkin, unfolds it and holds it up, but keeps it in his own hand. He tells the guards this is Mistress Corl's affair, concerning her dead brother's deed box, which is hers by right, with the letter sealed and signed to prove it. He says their masters can keep the wool, the barrels and the rats, and that the guards can watch you carry the one iron box out so nobody says you took a spoon. Sefa steps forward half a pace with her hands low and empty. She says the box belongs to Hesta Corl, that the guards know it, and that you only want to take what is hers and go.

A lantern hangs on a hook by the warehouse door, and the broad guard steps into its light so you can see he means it. Down the Coast Way a few forges are still going late, red mouths in the dark, hammers ringing out of time with each other.

He looks at the letter Pell holds up and doesn't reach for it. His lips move over the first line, slowly, then he gives up and looks at the seal. "That's her seal, right enough. Corl. I seen it on wool bales." He turns to you and takes in the shield, the stance, the way you stopped short with your hand off the hilt. Something in his face settles. "You've walked behind wagons."

Then he answers your question without hurrying. "Mr Oake. Dalmar Oake, the moneylender. He bought the dead man's paper, all of it, and he pays me to stand here. Nobody goes in. That's the whole of the order." He nods at Sefa. "You may be right that it's hers, mistress. I'm not the court. The court sits at dawn, and you can wave that letter at the magistrate there." He scratches his jaw. "And Oake's clerk came by at lamp-lighting and said it particular: nobody in the office. Not the lads, not me. So that box matters to somebody besides your mistress."

The thin one hasn't said a word yet. He hardly looks at the three of you. His eyes keep going south down the Way, toward where the street bends past a cooper's yard. When a boy's footsteps slap across the cobbles somewhere out of sight he stiffens, half turns, and sags again when nobody comes round the corner. He's wound tight, but not about you. He looks like a man waiting for somebody to arrive, and running out of patience.

"Gorm's told you," he says at last, short and flat, still looking down the street. "Oake keeps his counting-room on Smithy Row, over the chandler's. Go and bother him. He's likely abed." He shifts his weight. "And there's four more of us across the yard if you want to make a night of it."

He tips his head at the loading yard beside the warehouse. Across it, behind a low wall, stands a narrow two-storey lodging with one window lit and a shadow moving behind the shutter.

Gorm folds his arms, not unkindly, and leans back against the doorpost beside the bright new lock.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Anvar Corl's iron deed box
+ Quest: Anvar Corl's iron deed box

Where you are: outside the warehouse door on the Coast Way, facing the guards · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You tell Gorm you spent ten years behind wagons and say a plain order suits you. Then you glance toward the southern bend and ask the thin guard who he expects from that way, and whose business should come first if someone arrives for the office. You keep your tone matter-of-fact and your hands clear of your weapons.

Gorm nods slowly at the ten years. He says he did four, out of Nashkel, mostly iron, which doesn't run off in the night. That seems to be all the welcome he means to give.

The thin guard, Tobin, snaps his head round as if poked. For the first time he looks you straight in the face, and he looks annoyed, not caught. Nobody is coming for any office, he says, not from that way or any other. It's his own business and none of yours. He turns back to the bend before he's finished speaking. He never glances at the warehouse door, the shutter or the yard. You've stood enough night watches beside nervous men to read it: he is angry at being asked and angry at standing there. It isn't fear for the warehouse.

Gorm shifts against the doorpost and tells you quietly to leave him be, it isn't his day. He says nothing more about it.

Sefa, meanwhile, gives Gorm a small tired nod and says something about not making a night of it. She walks off down the street at an unhurried pace and tilts her head to beckon you. Pell, passing close by Tobin on his way after her, makes some small movement low at his hip. Tobin glances at the hand, frowns, and goes back to watching the road.

The lantern hisses on its hook. You are still at the warehouse door with Gorm and Tobin.

Where you are: at the warehouse door with Gorm and Tobin · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 3 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You tell Tobin that you meant no offence. "Aye," he says, to the road rather than to you. It's short, but it isn't a snap this time, and his shoulders come down a little. Gorm gives you the same slow nod he gave the ten years and settles back against the doorpost. The lantern stays on its hook beside him, lighting the street face and the bright new lock.

You nod to Gorm and walk south down the Coast Way, out of the yellow fan of light, following Sefa and Pell. The loading yard opens on your left as you pass the corner of the warehouse: a low wall and a pair of plank gates closed on a crossbar. A smithy boy notices iron whether he means to or not, and your eye catches the gate hinges. They're old, pitted strap-iron, but in the red spill from the working forge they shine wet. Someone has greased them, and not long ago. Behind the gates the yard is dark. Across it the lodging's one lit window throws a thin line of light where its shutter doesn't quite close.

The forge on the near side of the bend is still roaring. The two apprentices swap the hammer without missing a stroke, and neither looks up at a man in mail going by. You reach the black shadow of the cooper's wall, where the staves lean stacked against the stone and the hammering is loud enough to cover a low voice. Once out of easy earshot, you say your piece there, quietly: that Oake's clerk singled out the office, that you ought to hear why, that you'd rather not leave the warehouse unwatched, and you ask what they are thinking.

Behind you the warehouse door stands in its lantern light, with two men beside it. Past the bend the road south is still empty.

Where you are: In the shadow of the cooper's wall, south of the warehouse on the Coast Way · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 4 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You settle in against the cooper's wall with your shield turned in to your body, so the iron rim sits clear of the stone and makes no noise. The hammering from the forge carries your low words no farther than the stave-shadow.

From here you can see the whole of it. Gorm's lantern still makes its yellow fan on the street face, reaching the bright lock and thinning out toward the corner. Past the corner the downpipe runs down into black. If anything is moving up there against the timbers, the dark keeps it. You can't pick out more than the line of the beam-ends where the red glow from the forge touches them. The plank gates of the loading yard stand shut on their crossbar. Behind them the lodging's thin bar of light lies at its angle, and the shadow behind the shutter crosses it once, slowly, and goes back.

At the door Tobin has hardly moved. He's still facing south, which now means facing the bend and the cooper's wall. His eyes slide over the shadow where you stand without stopping on it. He's watching the road beyond.

Then, under the forge's rhythm, you hear something you've heard at the end of a thousand days on the Way: iron tyres on cobbles and the slow clop of one heavy horse. It's coming from the north, well up the Coast Way past the warehouse and not yet in sight. Far up the street a single lantern swings low and level, at about the height of a driver's bench, and comes on at a walking pace with no hurry in it.

Gorm hears it too. He pushes off the doorpost and turns his head to look up the street. Tobin doesn't turn at all.

Where you are: beside the cooper's wall, watching the warehouse and the street · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 5 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You keep your back to the cooper's stone and let the wagon come to you.

Wagons are your trade, and at this range you read it easily. It's a flat-bed with high sideboards, and the boards are bare: no house colours, no painted name, no Nashkel iron-mark, nothing a merchant would put on his own stock. The harness is plain leather with no brass on it. The big grey cob has feathered hooves and a chest built for heavy hauling, but it walks easily and the axle doesn't groan. The bed rides high on its springs, so it's empty. Somebody hired a strong horse and an empty wagon to collect a load at midnight. The heavy man in the leather hood drives like he's paid by the job, not by the house.

It doesn't turn toward the loading yard. It comes on into the door lantern's fan and stops short of Gorm, who has stepped into the road with the lantern held up. The smaller cloaked figure on the bench leans down toward him, and the hood stays up. Gorm's head turns from the bench to the yard gates and back. Over the hammering you can't hear a word of it.

Then, in the gap between one hammer-fall and the next, a small bell rings out across the yard: three quick, tinny strokes from the lodging. After it comes a man's voice, loud enough to cut through the forge, shouting that the high shutter is the one, and calling everyone up.

Lights come on behind the low wall, one, then another. A door bangs. Within a couple of minutes lanterns are bobbing in the loading yard, four of them, swinging at hip height the way men carry them when they've a cudgel in the other hand. They don't open the plank gates. They spread along the inside of the yard, and the lamplight slides over the canvas on the crates, the barred loading doors and the warehouse's yard wall, working toward the corner where the downpipe runs into the dark.

At the door Gorm calls out slow and loud, asking what the bell is. The carter hauls the cob back a step, and it stamps and blows. The cloaked figure doesn't sit back. It leans further down from the bench, one gloved hand chopping the air at Gorm, and the wagon stays where it is.

Tobin doesn't go to the yard. He doesn't even look at it. He comes off the doorpost and walks fast down the Coast Way, nearly at a run, out of the lantern light and south toward the bend and the cooper's wall. He's about sixty feet off and coming straight on, his eyes fixed on the dark road past the corner.

Where you are: against the cooper's wall on the Coast Way, south of the warehouse · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 6 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You step out of the shadow of the staves and swing wide of Tobin, who stands planted at the bend with his back to the warehouse. You walk north up the Coast Way at a road man's pace, shield on your arm, sword sheathed. The forge's red glow slides off your mail, and then Gorm's yellow lantern light takes its place.

Gorm has turned before you are halfway there. He stands at the wagon's front wheel with the lantern raised and watches you come, the way he'd watch a horse he didn't remember hitching. The carter keeps the cob's head short. You call out your question as you close the distance. The cloaked figure on the bench sits back as soon as your voice carries, and the hood turns a little toward you.

You step into the light and look up under the hood.

(A roll card for Bram Halloway, your character. Only you press it.)

[Roll card] Bram Halloway · Skill check — Perception: a look under the hood of the figure on the wagon bench, lit from below by Gorm's lantern
What adds to the die: +4 Perception
DC 15
Rerolls left: 2
The die is cast on the server; tap it to see how it fell.

[Roll the die]

(A roll card for Bram Halloway, your character. Only you press it.)

[Roll card] Bram Halloway · Skill check — Perception: a look under the hood of the figure on the wagon bench, lit from below by Gorm's lantern
What adds to the die: +4 Perception
DC 15
Rerolls left: 2
Die: 6
6 + 4 = 10
Failure — 10

[Onward] [Request an allowed reroll — Perception: a look under the hood of the figure on the wagon bench, lit from below by Gorm's lantern]

Before you leave the shadow, you tell Sefa quietly that you mean to see who is collecting a load.

The figure on the bench is quicker than your eyes. As you come into the light the hood dips and turns aside, toward the dark yard gates, so that Gorm's lantern lights only the cloth: good dark wool, damp at the hem, pulled well forward. You see no face and no hair, only a gloved hand that tugs the hood an inch lower and then rests on the bench rail. Whoever it is has done this before, keeping a face out of lantern light.

A voice comes from under the hood. It is low and even, with the careful vowels of someone who writes for a living, and it is aimed at Gorm, not at you. "Mr Hadley. Who is this man?"

Gorm doesn't answer her straight away. He lowers the lantern to chest height and looks at you, and the easy road-man warmth from before is gone from his face. He isn't hostile. He's working something out.

"Road man," he says to the bench, without looking round. "Came this evening with the Corl woman's letter. Him and two others." Then, to you, slowly: "Is that Oake's clerk." He lets it hang a moment and doesn't answer it. "Funny thing. You and your friends walk off down the street, and not a quarter hour later the bell goes on the high shutter." He looks past your shoulder toward the bend and the cooper's wall, then back. "Where's the other two got to?"

The carter shifts on the bench and keeps his eyes on his horse. The hood stays turned to the yard gates.

Up the Coast Way to the north, past the dark house fronts, Hob's lantern is coming back. It is held high like before, but it isn't alone now. Four or five more lights bob behind it at the same steady height, and boots strike the cobbles together, faint under the forge hammers. They are marching, not running, and they are still a long way off.

Where you are: In Gorm's lantern light by the wagon on the Coast Way, near the bench with the cloaked figure · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 7 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Gorm listens with the lantern held at chest height, and his face does not change when you mention the bell. When you turn the question on the wagon, his eyes go to the bench and stay there.

The hood does not turn toward you. The answer comes from under it in the same low, careful voice, pitched for Gorm as much as for you. She says she is Mr Oake's clerk, that Mr Oake holds every note on this building, and that until the court sits she speaks for him. Her name, she says, is no business of a hired man's. Her gloved hand lies still on the bench rail. As for removing goods, she says, nobody here has talked of removing anything except you.

The carter keeps his eyes on the cob's ears. For a moment the reins go slack in his fists, and he glances sideways at the hood like a man who has just heard his job described as something else.

Gorm is silent for a long breath. Then he says quietly to the bench: she asked him to open the yard gates, twice, and he said no to her as he said no to you. Nothing goes in, and nothing goes out either, not till the court. He sets his feet wider in the road, square between the wagon and the yard. He is on nobody's side but Oake's order as he understood it at lamp-lighting.

The voice from the bench stays even. "Mr Hadley. You'll be paid for tonight. Whether you're hired again is another matter." Gorm doesn't answer.

The marching boots are loud now even over the forge. Hob comes into the lantern light first, red in the face, his lamp held high, and five Flaming Fist spearmen follow in double file. Their tabards look rust-coloured in the bad light, each with the fist badge on the breast, and their helmets are dented but well kept. Last comes a grey-stubbled sergeant of about fifty with a short sword on his hip and no spear. He walks past you and Gorm as if you were bollards and stops at the wagon's front wheel.

"Mistress," he says, touching his helmet to the hood. He doesn't ask her name, and he doesn't look at the empty wagon bed. "Hob says you've had a bell."

She calls him Sergeant Tull. The bell rang on the high shutter, three strokes. She tips her head an inch toward you and says you and two others came to the door this evening with the Corl woman's letter, that Mr Hadley sent you off, and that within the quarter hour the bell rang. The other two, she says, have not been seen since.

Gorm opens his mouth and shuts it again. It is true as far as it goes, and he plainly knows it.

Tull turns and looks you over by the light of six lanterns: the mail, the shield, the sheathed sword, the road-worn boots. He takes his time. "Corl letter. That's paper for the magistrate at dawn, not for a warehouse at midnight." He jerks his chin without looking round and sends two men, Dace and Pruett, to the yard gate to let nobody through. Hallam and Orrin are to take a light down to the bend and find the other two, a man and a woman. He doesn't say which way. Hob is already pointing south, toward the forge and the cooper's wall.

Two spearmen go south down the Coast Way at a steady walk, their spearheads catching the forge's red glow. Two more plant their spear-butts in the dirt on either side of the plank gates. The fifth stays a long arm's reach from your shoulder, his spear upright and his eyes on your sword hand.

On the bench, the hood turns at last. Not toward you, but toward the yard gates and the two spearmen now standing at them.

Where you are: In the Coast Way street before the warehouse yard gates, beside the wagon, with Gorm and the Flaming Fist · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 8 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You keep your hands clear of your sword and tell Sergeant Tull that you asked at the door, accepted Gorm's refusal, and came back openly when the bell rang. You say you'll stay while he looks into it. You ask him to keep Gorm's whole account: the clerk asked him twice to open the yard gates for this wagon and threatened his work when he refused. You ask that Gorm not lose his place for saying so. Then you ask Tull straight out whether you are detained or may take your claim to Oake.

Tull hears you out without interrupting. At the words about asking twice, he turns his head slowly toward Gorm.

"That so, Hadley?"

"Twice." Gorm doesn't look at the bench. "That's so."

For a moment nobody speaks. The forge rings down the street. The carter studies his cob's ears like a man who wishes he were elsewhere. On the bench the hood doesn't move, but the gloved hand on the rail has closed around it.

"Then you kept your order," Tull says to Gorm. "Good. Now it's mine." He looks you over again, as if the answer were written on your mail. "You're not taken up. You're not walking off either. You stay where Orrin can reach you till my lads come back from the bend with your friends, or without them. Then we'll see." He glances up the dark street. "And nobody's knocking up a moneylender at midnight over a letter. Your claim waits for the magistrate, same as his."

He jerks his chin toward the yard without looking round. "Dace. Pruett. Open the gates. Wagon goes in off the street. It's blocking the Way." He raises his voice a little, for Gorm and you as much as for his men. "Gates shut behind it. Nothing comes out of that yard till the court sits. My word on it."

"Thank you, Sergeant Tull." The clerk's voice is as even as before. "Mr Oake will be glad the yard is secured."

Gorm opens his mouth, then looks at the five rust-red tabards and the sergeant's short sword and shuts it. He steps back against the doorpost under the lantern. He hasn't stood aside so much as been moved aside, and his face says he knows it. Before he settles, his eyes find yours for a moment. It isn't warm, but it isn't the wary look from before either. It's the look one road man gives another when they've both watched the boss make a bad call.

Dace and Pruett lift the crossbar off the plank gates. The greased hinges make no sound. The carter clicks his tongue, the big grey cob leans into the collar, and the empty wagon turns off the Coast Way and rolls into the yard, iron tyres crunching on straw. The hood never looks back. The gates swing shut and the bar drops into place. Dace and Pruett plant their spear-butts again, outside the gates now, facing the street.

Over the low wall, lantern light moves in the yard. Someone calls a short question, and the corner man answers. Then you hear a sound you know from a hundred loading yards: the dull knock of a brick dropped on beaten earth, then another, then a third. They're taking the weights off the canvas.

Down at the bend the patrol's lantern has stopped at the cooper's wall. From here you can see only the light, held head-high at the stacked staves, and two spearheads catching the forge's red glow beside it.

Your records, changed:

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: The wagon in the Corl yard

Where you are: outside the yard gates on the Coast Way, under Orrin's watch · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 9 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You tell the sergeant, loudly enough to carry over the sound of the forge, that the men inside are lifting weights off the canvas and seem to be preparing a load. You ask whether he will put one of his own men inside to see that his word is kept, since a man outside a shut gate cannot witness what goes onto the wagon. You keep your hands where they were, in plain view.

Then you turn your head a little toward the low wall and listen for what follows from the yard.

The forge rings like a bell-tower. The apprentices have pulled a fresh bar from the fire and set both hammers going on it, one after the other, and every word behind the low wall is lost in the noise. You can make out lantern light sliding across the top of the wall. Once, between two strokes, you hear the hollow knock of something heavy set down on planking. You can't tell whether a crate went onto the wagon bed or came off the stack, and you can't make out any voice well enough to say who is speaking.

Sergeant Tull doesn't look toward the yard. He keeps his eyes on you and lets your question sit a breath longer than it needs. Then he says his men stand where he puts them. Two spears on a barred gate are witness enough for the magistrate, he says, and will do for you. He hooks a thumb back over his shoulder without turning. The mistress, he says, is setting the stock in order for the court's count, off the wet ground and onto boards. A crate on a wagon bed is the same crate it was on the straw, and the court counts it either way.

Gorm steps off the doorpost, only a step into the lantern fan, and speaks to Tull rather than to you, slowly and carefully. He says he could stand in the yard. He is Oake's man, and if anything goes short at the count, it's him they'll ask.

Tull answers without raising his voice. Gorm has a door, he says, and should mind it.

Gorm looks at him a moment longer. Then he steps back to the doorpost, but this time he doesn't lean on it. He stands upright beside the bright new lock with his arms at his sides and his face turned toward the yard gates.

Orrin, the spearman at your shoulder, shifts his grip on his spear. For half a heartbeat his eyes go to the sergeant's back and then come away. He looks like a man who has heard an order he wouldn't have given himself and won't say so.

Out at the gates Dace and Pruett face the street and stand like posts. The lantern glow over the yard brightens, dims as someone carries a light past the wall, and brightens again. Down at the bend the search lantern has left the cooper's staves and is moving north up the middle of the Coast Way, held head-high.

Where you are: Outside the forge yard, before the shut gate, facing Sergeant Tull · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 10 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You tell Tull you will give the magistrate an account of what you saw and leave the counting to him. Tull gives you a short nod, like a man taking what he expected to win. "Do that," he says, and turns away toward the street.

You leave it there. You keep your hands clear and your feet where they are, with Orrin's spear upright an arm's length from your shoulder. You watch the search lantern come up the middle of the Coast Way out of the forge's red spill.

There are two spearmen and one lantern, with Sefa a step ahead of it, her hands held out from her sides. Nobody has hold of her. You look past them down the road, then along the dark house fronts on both sides, and find nobody else. There is no fourth shape at the edge of the light and nobody walking behind. Pell isn't with them. Hallam steps into the fan of Gorm's lantern and makes his report to the sergeant, short and flat: the woman was hiding in the cooper's staves, and there was no sign of the man. Tull turns to look Sefa over.

Gorm is only a few paces off, upright at the doorpost. You don't move toward him. Under the hammering, you quietly ask whether he knows the clerk's name.

Gorm doesn't turn his head. He keeps watching the yard gates. "Her name." He thinks about it longer than the question needs, like a man deciding what he owes and to whom. "Venn. Mr Oake calls her Venn. Never heard no front to it." A pause. "She ain't been with him long. Since after the thaw. Before that it was old Pelham kept his books, and Pelham never come out at night for nothing."

Orrin, at your shoulder, is close enough to have heard every word. His eyes stay on your sword hand, and he says nothing.

Behind the low wall the glow over the yard shifts and settles closer to the loading doors. Between two hammer-falls you hear a sound you've heard at the start of a thousand mornings: iron rattling on iron, a tether ring knocking against a wall staple as a lead rope comes off it, and then the big cob shaking itself in its harness so every buckle jingles. Gorm hears it too. His jaw sets, and he keeps his eyes on the gates.

Where you are: outside the forge on the Coast Way, near Gorm, Orrin and Tull · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 11 — what does Bram Halloway do?

messages.text:
I stop a few paces short of the men, keeping my sword sheathed.

“Aye. Hesta Corl sent us for her iron deed box from her brother’s office. We’ve a letter of claim.” I nod toward Pell. “Not here to shift wool or empty the place. Who’s authorised to let us collect it?”

While we talk, I keep an eye on the thin guard and the stretch of street he’s watching.

“Ten years behind wagons,” I tell Gorm. “Long enough to appreciate a plain order.”

I glance toward the southern bend, then back to the thin guard. “But you’ve scarcely looked at us. Who are you expecting from that way? If someone’s coming for the office, we’d best settle whose business takes precedence before they arrive.”

I keep my tone matter-of-fact and my hands clear of my weapons, watching how he takes the question.

“Fair enough. No offence meant,” I tell Tobin, then nod to Gorm and follow Sefa and Pell.

Once we’re out of easy earshot, I lower my voice. “Oake’s clerk singled out the office. We ought to hear why, though I’d rather not leave this place unwatched. What are you thinking?”

“The yard gate’s been greased recently,” I add quietly. “Might be ordinary upkeep, but worth watching along with that loose upper shutter.”

I settle beside the cooper’s wall where I can watch the warehouse without standing in the road, shield held close so it doesn’t scrape the stone. I look for movement at the yard gates and upper shutter while listening to Pell and Sefa.

“Wagon coming from the north,” I murmur. “Let’s see where it stops.”

I stay against the wall and watch it approach, looking for any merchant’s mark and whether the driver turns toward the loading yard. I keep the yard gates in view as well—particularly anyone coming out to meet it.

“I’m going to see who’s collecting a load,” I say quietly to Sefa.

I step out of the shadow, leaving Tobin room to pass without blocking him, and walk briskly back toward Gorm. My sword stays sheathed.

“Gorm! You’ve men shouting about an open shutter and an empty wagon at your door. Is that Oake’s clerk on the bench?”

I look up at the cloaked figure as I approach, trying to get a clear view beneath the hood.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“I left Sefa by the cooper’s wall. Pell can answer for himself,” I say. “I heard the bell from the street, same as you.”

I stop a few paces from Gorm, keeping clear of the horse.

“You told us nobody goes in, and particularly not into the office. Now there’s an empty wagon here and someone keeping her face hidden. Before you put this on us, ask what she’s come to take.”

I look toward the bench. “Bram Halloway. Hesta Corl hired me to collect her deed box. Who are you, and have you authority to remove goods before the court sits?”

I keep my hands still and away from my sword.

“Sergeant, I asked at the door and accepted Gorm’s refusal. I came back openly when the bell rang. I’ll stay here while you look into it.”

I nod toward Gorm. “But keep his whole account: this clerk asked him twice to open the yard gates for this wagon, and threatened his work when he refused. He’s held to his orders. Don’t let him lose his place for telling you so.”

Then I address Tull directly. “Are we being detained, or may we take our claim to Oake?”

“Sergeant. They’re lifting the weights off the canvas in there. Sounds like they’re preparing a load.”

I stay where I am, hands clear.

“You’ve given your word nothing comes out. Will you put one of your men inside to see it kept? Outside a shut gate, he can’t witness what goes onto that wagon.”

I listen for further sounds from the yard while keeping Tull in view.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The Coast Way smells of coal smoke and hot iron, and the ring of Beregost's hammers never quite stops. Ahead stands the Corl warehouse, its broad door fastened with a heavy new lock that is still bright. Two men lean beside it in the creditors' service. One is a broad, patient fellow with a cudgel at his belt. The other is thinner and keeps glancing up and down the street as if he expects someone.

Pell Dunmore carries Hesta Corl's letter of claim, which the three of you share, along with her promise of 60 gold once the iron deed box reaches her hands. Bram Halloway's chain mail and shield draw the thin guard's eye at once. Your quiet bearing earns a second look from the broad one. Somewhere inside is Anvar Corl's office, and in it, if all is as Hesta says, the box. Nightfall is the deadline, and at dawn the creditors' court sits.

High on the warehouse wall, one shutter hangs a finger's width open where every other is shut fast. The broad guard pushes himself off the wall and looks the three of you over. "Warehouse is closed by order of the creditors," he says. "You've business here?"

Where you are: Coast Way, before the Corl warehouse door · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 1 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram stops a few paces short of the guards, his sword still sheathed. He says Hesta Corl sent you all to fetch her brother's iron deed box from his office, that you carry a letter of claim, and that you haven't come to haul away the wool or strip the place. He asks who has the authority to let you collect it. Pell, half a step behind him with his hands loose and empty, draws the letter out of his jerkin and holds it up open, without passing it over. He tells the guards it is Mistress Corl's business, the box hers by right, the letter sealed and signed. He says their masters are welcome to the wool, the barrels and the rats, and that the guards can watch you carry out the one iron box so nobody can claim you pocketed a spoon.

A lantern hangs on a hook by the warehouse door, and the broad guard steps into its light so you can see he means it. Down the Coast Way a few forges are still going late, red mouths in the dark, hammers ringing out of time with each other.

He looks at the letter Pell holds up and doesn't reach for it. His lips move over the first line, slowly, then he gives up and looks at the seal. "That's her seal, right enough. Corl. I seen it on wool bales." He turns to Bram and takes in the shield, the stance, the way Bram stopped short with his hand off the hilt. Something in his face settles. "You've walked behind wagons."

Then he answers what was asked, without hurrying. "Mr Oake. Dalmar Oake, the moneylender. He bought the dead man's paper, all of it, and he pays me to stand here. Nobody goes in. That's the whole of the order." He nods at you. "You may be right that it's hers, mistress. I don't say you're not. I'm not the court. The court sits at dawn, and you can wave that letter at the magistrate there." He scratches his jaw. "And Oake's clerk came by at lamp-lighting and said it particular: nobody in the office. Not the lads, not me. So that box matters to somebody besides your mistress."

The thin one hasn't said a word yet. He hardly looks at the three of you. His eyes keep going south down the Way, toward where the street bends past a cooper's yard. When a boy's footsteps slap across the cobbles somewhere out of sight he stiffens, half turns, and sags again when nobody comes round the corner. He's wound tight, but not about you. He looks like a man waiting for somebody to arrive, and running out of patience.

"Gorm's told you," he says at last, short and flat, still looking down the street. "Oake keeps his counting-room on Smithy Row, over the chandler's. Go and bother him. He's likely abed." He shifts his weight. "And there's four more of us across the yard if you want to make a night of it."

He tips his head at the loading yard beside the warehouse. Across it, behind a low wall, stands a narrow two-storey lodging with one window lit and a shadow moving behind the shutter.

Gorm folds his arms, not unkindly, and leans back against the doorpost beside the bright new lock.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Anvar Corl's iron deed box
+ Quest: Anvar Corl's iron deed box

Where you are: outside the warehouse door on the Coast Way, facing the guards · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 2 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You hold Gorm's eye, give a small tired nod, and say you won't make a night of it. Then you walk a few unhurried steps along the street and tilt your head to beckon Bram and Pell, as though the three of you have decided to leave.

Gorm seems content to see you go. Pell follows. As he passes the thin guard he makes some small movement low at his hip, out of the light. The guard, Tobin, glances at the hand with the frown a man gives a stranger scratching himself, and goes back to watching the road. Bram stays by the lantern, and what passes between him and the guards doesn't carry to you.

Down the Way the street bends past the cooper's yard. A forge on the near side is still working, its doors open on a red glow, two apprentices taking turns on a big piece of iron. The hammering is steady enough to cover anything said quietly. You stop in the black shadow of the cooper's wall, where stacked staves and hoop-iron lean against the stone, and Pell joins you. You speak your piece low and he answers with his. Neither carries back to the warehouse over the hammers.

From this corner the yard side of the Corl warehouse is in view in a way it wasn't from the door. Gorm's lantern lights the street face in a yellow fan. It reaches the open shutter but thins out short of the corner. Past that, the downpipe runs down into true dark on the yard side, where the loading yard opens behind a low wall and a pair of plank gates. Across the yard the lodging still has its one lit window. As you watch, the shadow behind that shutter passes once, stops, and passes back. Somebody over there is awake and moving about.

South of you, past the bend, the Coast Way runs empty toward the edge of town. A dog barks somewhere among the yards, and nobody comes.

Bram is still at the warehouse door with Gorm and Tobin.

Where you are: in the shadow of the cooper's yard wall · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 3 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You ease back against the shadowed wall and let the forge's hammering cover you while you take stock of the street. Bram stands still by the lantern, Gorm's shoulders are in view, and the lit lodging window beyond the low wall has a shadow passing behind it. Under the noise you tell Pell that one person across the yard is awake and that a shout would finish you before you start. You say the shutter is no use to you, but you can follow where he goes. If you are seen, you would rather be taken for something holy than for thieves. You ask how he means to reach it quietly.

Pell answers low. Bram is still at the door, and Gorm is happy talking wagons. He tells you to stay here, where you can watch both the bend and the lit window. If anyone comes round the corner or the lodging door opens, you are to give one short whistle, and two if it is trouble. At two he will go quiet and stay put until it passes. If it all goes wrong, he says he will return along the yard side and find you in this same spot. He pulls his hood up and leaves the stave-shadow.

He does not go back through the lantern light. He crosses to the far side of the Coast Way, where the house fronts are dark, and drifts away along them in short stops and starts. Then he is lost to you in the dark toward the loading yard.

Down at the forge the apprentices stop. The big piece of iron goes into the trough with a long hiss and a gout of steam. For three or four heartbeats the Coast Way is quiet enough that you hear the lantern hissing at the warehouse door, the dog somewhere among the yards, and your own breath. Behind the lodging shutter the shadow stops. Then the tongs ring on the anvil, the hammers start again, and the shadow moves on.

You stand in the stave-shadow at the cooper's wall with the bend in front of you. The road south is still empty, and no foot has come round it.

Where you are: in the stave-shadow at the cooper's wall on the Coast Way, watching the bend and the lit window · Time: Day 1 · night

Round 4 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You keep to the dark beside the stave-stack, your shoulders still against the wood, and let your eyes make their slow rounds. Your right hand rests on the cord of your prayer beads.

The bend south is empty. The road past it runs pale under the stars to the last houses of town, and nothing moves on it but a cat crossing from one yard wall to the next. The forge glow comes and goes on the cobbles as the apprentices lift and drop the hammer. Across the loading yard the lodging window still holds its thin bar of light. Up at the warehouse corner, where Pell should be, you see black timber, a blacker downpipe and nothing else. If he's there, the dark is keeping him.

At the door, the lantern shows two men: Gorm, broad against the doorpost, and Tobin facing south toward you. Tobin's gaze passes over the cooper's wall and doesn't stop. He's looking at the road behind you.

Then you see a light where there wasn't one: north, up the Coast Way past the warehouse. It is a single lantern, low and level, swinging a little and coming at a walking pace. Under the hammering you can just make out iron tyres grinding on cobbles and the heavy clop of one horse. Over two or three minutes it comes into the edge of the door lantern's light: a flat-bed wagon with high sideboards, drawn by a big grey cob with feathered hooves. The driver is a heavy man in a leather hood, bent over the reins. A second figure sits beside him on the bench, smaller and wrapped in a dark cloak with the hood up. From the way the cloak falls, you think it may be a woman, but at this distance you can't be sure.

Gorm has stepped off the doorpost and out into the road with his lantern raised. The wagon stops short of him. The cloaked figure leans down from the bench to speak, and Gorm scratches his jaw. You can't hear a word over the forge, only see Gorm's head turning from the cloaked figure to the yard gates and back. Tobin hasn't turned round at all.

You turn your head toward the wagon, then to the widening shutter, then back to the road. You put two fingers to your lips and give two short, low whistles, pitched to carry under the forge-hammers as far as the warehouse corner and no farther. Then you ease back among the staves until the hoop-iron is cold against your shoulder, and you keep still, watching the yard and the new arrivals.

Almost on top of your second whistle, a small bell rings across the yard: three quick, thin strokes. It is faint at this distance, but you hear it clearly in the gap between two hammer-falls. Then a man's voice comes from the lodging, loud enough to carry over the forge: "The high one! That's the high shutter! Up, the lot of you, up!" More lights come on behind the low wall, first downstairs and then a second one. A door bangs. Within a couple of minutes, lanterns are moving in the loading yard. There are four of them, carried at hip height and swinging. They don't open the plank gates. They spread out along the inside of the yard, and their light slides over the canvas on the crates and the barred loading doors, then up the warehouse's yard wall toward the dark corner by the downpipe. You watch the corner and see black timber and black iron, and nothing that moves.

At the door Gorm's voice carries, slow and loud: "What's that? What's the bell?" The carter hauls his cob back a step, and the big horse stamps and blows. The cloaked figure on the bench doesn't sit back. It leans farther down toward Gorm, and a gloved hand cuts the air between them, once and then again. The wagon stays where it is.

Then Tobin leaves the door. He doesn't go toward the yard or even look at it. He comes straight down the Coast Way, fast, nearly at a run, out of the lantern light and into the forge's red spill, coming right at the bend and the cooper's wall. You keep still in the dark by the cooper's wall, moving only your eyes. You give the smallest shake of your head toward the shadow behind you, but nobody is there to see it. Bram's low words had reached you a moment earlier: he meant to see who was collecting a load. By the time your chin moved he was already out of the staves' shadow. He swung wide of Tobin, red forge light on his mail and then the yellow of Gorm's lantern, and walked north up the Coast Way with his sword sheathed. The shadow beside you is empty now, with only the cold hoop-iron and the smell of new-cut oak. Your thumb rests on a wooden bead, and you count the distance as you wait.

The lanterns in the yard have stopped moving. One lamp is left at the downpipe corner, held low, with a man's shape beside it looking up at the high shutter. The other lights have gone inside the warehouse or out through the gate. The yard behind the low wall is darker than it was a minute ago. There is no light on the black timbers by the shutter and nothing moving on them.

At the door, Bram steps into the lantern fan beside the wagon. You can't hear a word over the hammers. You see the hood on the bench turn away from him toward the yard gates. Far up the Coast Way to the north there are lights where there weren't any before. One is held high in front, and four or five more follow it at the same steady height, bobbing together. They are still small with distance, but they are getting bigger.

A few strides south of you, Tobin is still at the bend with his hands on his hips. His breathing has slowed. He hasn't looked back again.

Then running feet slap up the pale road from the last houses. A boy of ten or eleven comes round the bend with a shawl flapping round his shoulders like a cape, and he nearly runs into Tobin.

The boy cries out that his mam says Mr Reeve is to come, and that it's now, and he's not to stop for anything. Tobin grabs him by both shoulders and begins to ask if she is all right, if it is happening. The boy only says again that his mam says now, as if that answers everything. He pulls free and starts back the way he came.

You stay in the black mouth of the stave-stack until Tobin's running footsteps fade away south among the last houses and stop being a sound at all. You wait a few breaths longer to be sure. Then you edge along the cooper's wall a few inches at a time, the staves cold against your shoulder, your breath even and one hand at your side, near the dagger but not on it. Near the end of the stack the shadow goes grey where the forge's red spill reaches it, and you stop just short of that. You rise only far enough to look out through a gap between two staves, and your night-eyes do the rest.

The lights from the north have reached the door. Hob's lamp is the first you pick out, still held high, and Gorm's lantern is on its hook. You count five more, and under them helmets and spearheads catch the light. The men wear tabards that look rust-red in this light, each with a stitched badge on the breast: the Flaming Fist, five spearmen. A sixth man carries no spear and walks past everyone else to stand at the wagon's front wheel. The others give him room, so he must be their sergeant.

Bram stands in the middle of it all, a few paces from Gorm, his shield on his arm and his sword sheathed. One spearman stands close beside him, an arm's length from his shoulder, and doesn't move.

The hammering drowns out every word. You see the sergeant look Bram up and down, taking his time. Then Hob turns and points with his whole arm down the Coast Way, past the forge, at the bend and the cooper's wall. He is pointing at the stack you're standing behind.

Two spearmen go to the yard's plank gates and plant their spear-butts on either side. Two more take a lantern and come south.

They walk steadily, without hurrying, side by side down the middle of the street, the lantern swinging between them. When they come into the forge's glow their spearheads turn red. The apprentices glance up for the first time all night, then go back to their iron. One spearman lifts the lantern to head height and throws its light ahead of them across the cobbles. It reaches the far house fronts and then the near ones, sweeping from side to side.

In a gap between two hammer-falls, a young voice carries clearly from the nearer of the two: a man and a woman, he said, by the barrels. The other answers that it means the staves, the cooper's.

They are about forty feet off and coming straight on. The lantern light slides along the base of the cooper's wall, over hoop-iron and the first of the staves, toward the end of the stack where the shadow is already thin.

You touch the beads once and step out of the shadow before the lantern can find you. Your hands are open and low, your chin up, and you walk into the light along the wall as if you had been going somewhere. You tell the nearer spearman, calmly and loud enough for him to hear, that you are the woman from the warehouse, and that you came back this way because the road ahead is darker than you like.

The lantern jerks up to your face. Both spearheads come down a hand's breadth. They don't level at you, but they no longer point at the sky.

For a breath the cracked bead under your thumb is warm, like lamp-glass just after the flame goes out. Then it is only wood again.

The story doesn't hold. The nearer spearman is young, with a soft jaw under a dented helmet. He holds the lantern and looks from you to the staves and back. He watched the light slide along that wall, and he watched you come out of the dark at the end of it, not down the road.

"Came back from where?" he says. "You come out of them staves, mistress. I seen you."

The older one beside him is lean and pocked, with a spear held easily in one hand. He doesn't answer you. He looks past your shoulder into the stave-shadow you just left. "The woman from the warehouse," he repeats, as if he were writing it down. "That's what Hob said. Man and a woman, gone off down here, and then the bell." He jerks his head at the young one. "Look in the stack. The man's tall, he'll—" He stops, frowns, and starts again. "Look for the man. Hallam's going nowhere till you do."

The young one hands the lantern to the older man, Hallam, and walks the length of the staves. He jabs his spear-butt into the gaps and kicks the hoop-iron so it rings. At the far end he leans round the corner of the cooper's wall and looks at the bend and the empty pale road south. He comes back shaking his head. "Nobody. Just her."

"Then she'll do for now." Hallam gives you a look without much in it, the look of a man who was sent to fetch something and has found half of it. "Sergeant wants a word with you at the door. You walk in front, hands where I can see them. You've got a knife there. Leave it be."

They don't take hold of you. The young one falls in on your left and Hallam on your right, half a step behind, with the lantern held up so it lights your back. The three of you turn north up the Coast Way, into the forge's red spill and out of it. Up ahead a lantern burns on its hook by the warehouse door. Men stand around it: spears, the sergeant's grey head, and a broad shape in mail. Behind the low wall of the yard, lantern light moves, and something heavy thumps onto a wagon bed.
